After three years of regional war, this is a battle Israel always knew was coming.
The general election on Tuesday hangs over a country that's deeply divided and ready for a fight.
Polls published on Friday put the governing coalition and the main opposition bloc almost neck-and-neck, with half a million first-time voters due to cast their ballot and some 70,000 Israelis reportedly flying in from abroad specifically to vote.
On Saturday night, vast crowds of opposition voters gathered in central Tel Aviv to demand a change of government.
"We're optimistic," 21-year-old Omri told me. "I want peace, I want security, and I want to end corruption and get the religious fanatics out."
This campaign has been energized by new tactics - including AI videos designed to grab the headlines - and also by a new face.
Gadi Eisenkot is, perhaps, not the man you might expect to take on the flashy, aggressive, media-savvy brand of Israel's longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
Relatively new to politics, with a working-class Moroccan background, Eisenkot is a former military chief of staff who is renowned for his calm manner and low-drama approach. He's been dubbed by some as a "non-politician".
But he and his centrist Yashar party have regularly pipped Netanyahu and his Likud party to the top spot in recent polls, the last of which was published on Friday, in line with Israeli election law.
Israeli politics is the art of coalition-building, rather than the task of any one party winning power, but with the predicted result too close to call, Eisenkot's rising profile has sharpened a race many Israelis already see as existential for the future of their country.
I watched him slip past the cameras at a community centre for Ethiopian Jews in the city of Ramle last week, through a gaggle of security personnel and advisors.
One of those who had come to hear him speak was David, a smartly dressed man in a freshly-pressed shirt and navy jacket, who said he had met Eisenkot before.
"He looks you in the eye, not like a leader looking down at someone," David told me. "And he listens. He's very sympathetic."
Eisenkot's appeal is often put down to his personal manner and profile. A softly-spoken military man whose son was killed during the Gaza War, he has presented himself as coming "from the periphery", not from Israel's wealthy urban elite.
His Moroccan background became election headlines earlier this month when a pro-Netanyahu speaker used a racist slur to refer to Eisenkot during a TV debate, referring to him as a Moroccan "monkey".
"These elections are about many issues," Eisenkot told the crowd gathered at the Ramle community centre. "They are about security, economy, education...but primarily, they are about the identity of the State of Israel, and what kind of Israel we want to see. A Jewish state, a democratic state, a liberal, tolerant, egalitarian state."
This is music to opposition ears, who say Benjamin Netanyahu's government is a threat to Israel's democracy, pointing to his efforts to curb the powers of the judicial system, and his refusal to establish a state commission of inquiry into the 7 October 2023 attacks on the grounds that the country's Supreme Court would be biased against him.
Eisenkot, along with other opposition leaders, has attempted to draw voters away from Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party by promising such a state inquiry, which a recent survey suggests is supported by more than 70% of Jewish Israelis.
He has also vowed to enforce court rulings on drafting ultra-Orthodox Jews into national military service - another measure that is popular with right-wing voters and opposition alike.
Benjamin Netanyahu has hit back with a campaign focused on Israel's security, and a core campaign slogan of "No Surrender".
He has repeatedly cast his rivals as soft on security, playing on the fears of some right-wing voters that Jewish opposition parties might ally with Israel's Arab parties to secure a majority, and suggesting this could compromise national security.
Around one-fifth of Israel's population is Arab - many of whom describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.
These are the first elections since the 7 October attacks, in which Hamas-led gunmen stormed through Gaza's border fence, killing almost people and taking 251 hostage.
It was Israel's worst security failure, but three years on its prime minister is again running for re-election as the only man who can keep Israel safe.
"If the army had woken him in time, it wouldn't have happened," Shlomi Bashar told me, one of several die-hard Netanyahu fans drinking in a basement cafÃ© in Jerusalem's Mahane Yehuda market. "He does bear a certain responsibility, but after the 7 October, he changed the entire Middle East."
Netanyahu has been hammering home the message that Israel's wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, in the years after the 7 October attacks, have reduced existential threats to the country.
"We need him to be re-elected so that he can finish this work," said Shlomi. "In my opinion, he is one of the best leaders in the world. Most of the world loves him and respects him, because he is a strong man and his ideas are correct."
The prime minister has traditionally relied on a stable base of right-wing voters, but is projected to see a thinning of support in this election. Some voters may be slipping away to opposition parties like Eisenkot's. Others, including some die-hard Likud voters we spoke to, said the 7 October attacks had pushed them towards parties further on the right.
Lt Col (Res) Eyal Hajbi, head of the regional civil defence unit in the Netanyahu stronghold of Sderot, right on the Gaza border, lost several friends and colleagues in the attacks. He lights candles for them every day in his office, and told me he would be thinking about them when he cast his ballot on Tuesday.

Serbia's long-standing leader Aleksandar VuÄiÄ has admitted defeat to the student-led protest movement in snap parliamentary elections.
"We still do not have final results... it is clear that we have lost these elections," the right-wing populist leader said as he conceded late on Sunday.
Preliminary figures provided by Serbia's election commission indicated a record high turnout, which commentators had suggested would favour the student movement.
VuÄiÄ had called the snap elections after two years of protests triggered by the 2024 collapse of a train station canopy in the city of Novi Sad, which killed 16 and was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence in Serbia.
VuÄiÄ had spent two terms as president and could not seek a third term, so was leading his party with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.
He made his announcement at the headquarters of his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the capital Belgrade.
There were celebrations on the streets of the city, with people dancing and chanting "victory", cars honking, and fireworks set off. "Serbia is free," one student told the BBC. "It's a miracle."
The Student List - which has no obvious leaders and whose members are not used to politics - had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia.
It decided to field candidates to the 250-member parliament from across Serbian society including doctors, actors, academics and sports personalities.
"This will be a free state," its lead candidate - cardiologist Ilija SrdanoviÄ - said in a statement to BBC Serbian as the result became clear.
He said the movement hoped to "free the country from tyranny".
The anti-corruption movement campaigned on a manifesto that included purging officials who broke rules cracking down on protesters, stopping party loyalists from leading public enterprises, and freeing the public broadcaster of political control.
VuÄiÄ and the SNS party have repeatedly denied corruption.
VuÄiÄ, who backs Serbia's candidacy for the European Union while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, had pledged to increase pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare.
Preliminary figures provided by Serbia's election commission suggested a record high turnout, with 64.9% having cast their vote by 18:00 local time (17:00 GMT), two hours before polls were set to close.

Israeli voters are preparing to head to the polls in an election some have described as the most consequential in the country's history.

72a889c4ad54.text: By — Mike Catalini, Associated Press Mike Catalini, Associated Press By — Mike Householder, Associated Press Mike Householder, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-escalates-rhetoric-against-el-sayed-as-he-tries-to-undermine-democrat-in-michigan-senate-race Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump escalates rhetoric against El-Sayed as he tries to undermine Democrat in Michigan Senate race Politics Oct 25, 2026 5:50 PM EDT PORT HURON, Mich. (AP) — President Donald Trump escalated his attacks against Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday with rhetoric that questioned the Muslim candidate's loyalties to the U.S. and repeatedly tried to tie him to extremism, claims the Democrat has repeatedly denied and denounced. "Over the past three weeks, I've traveled all over the country. But I'm here today in Michigan for a very important reason," Trump told the crowd in Port Huron. "I'm here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The Republican president has been attacking El-Sayed's faith throughout the campaign and claiming his past statements and background show a sympathy for extremists. El-Sayed, a former public health official, has repeatedly said he is loyal to the U.S. and disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamic movement with branches that the U.S. government has designated as terrorist organizations. The claims by Republicans have been denounced by Democrats as attacks on El-Sayed's faith and his Egyptian heritage. El-Sayed would be the first Muslim senator if elected. Trump's return to Michigan reflects the importance of the race. Republicans see an opening to flip a Senate seat as they try to hold onto the majority in the chamber. El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman backed by Trump, in the Nov. 3 race to succeed retiring Democrat Gary Peters. The race has taken on significance beyond Michigan, with Republicans casting El-Sayed as a symbol of a Democratic Party moving further to the left. Progressives, meanwhile, see his candidacy as a test of whether their agenda can win in a battleground state ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Trump invokes 9/11 when talking about El-Sayed Trump on Sunday invoked the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, drawing a comparison between stopping El-Sayed from entering the Senate and the passengers who fought back against the hijackers aboard United Flight 93. "Twenty-five years later, Michigan needs to stand up and fight, just like Todd did, to stop a jihadist from walking into the Capitol," Trump said, referring to Todd Beamer, a Michigan native who died aboard the flight. Trump then invited Beamer's parents onto the stage. READ MORE: Obama, in Midwest, assails 'cruelty' and indecency from Trump and his allies in the midterm campaign Trump's visit to Port Huron follows former Democratic President Barack Obama's appearances Saturday in Michigan and Ohio for his party's candidates. It is Trump's latest stop on a packed campaign schedule to bolster Republicans on the midterm ballot as the GOP is weighed down by voters' frustration with the economy and the war with Iran. Port Huron, about 60 miles (96.56 kilometers) northeast of Detroit, sits across the St. Clair River from Canada, where Trump's tariffs have strained trade relations between the longtime allies. Unlike Trump's earlier trips to Republican-controlled states where his party is on defense, the GOP has not won a Senate race in Michigan for more than three decades. Rogers unsuccessfully ran for Senate in 2024, losing to then-Rep. Elissa Slotkin. El-Sayed has taunted Trump, encouraging him to come to Michigan in the belief that a visit would backfire on Rogers. "Donald, if you're watching, don't wuss out, man," El-Sayed said. The progressive, who won a divisive primary in August, has said the country needs to "turn the page on Donald Trump." The campaign has been one of the most contentious this year During their second and final general election campaign debate, Rogers questioned El-Sayed's loyalty to the United States. "Are you for America, or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?" Rogers asked. El-Sayed said that questioning was "shameful." "I'm proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray," he said. READ MORE: In final Michigan Senate debate, El-Sayed and Rogers question each other's loyalties Speaking before Trump's appearance Sunday, Rogers repeated his allegations linking El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood. "The Muslim Brotherhood celebrated exactly one victory in the United States in the primary this year," Rogers said on stage. "Abdul El-Sayed's." El-Sayed has faced criticism for his own rhetoric, particularly when he said "hurt people hurt people" after an attack on a synagogue in the Detroit area. The attacker had lost four relatives in an Israeli airstrike on Lebanon the week earlier. El-Sayed later apologized, saying he was not trying to justify what happened. "To anyone who feels like my comments might have been hurtful, I'm really sorry," he said. "That was not my intention." El-Sayed has struggled to unite Democrats following a contentious primary against Rep. Haley Stevens. Appearing Sunday on CNN, Stevens declined to explicitly say whether she was "still fully behind" El-Sayed, instead saying she was "on the team" and naming other Michigan Democratic candidates but not the party's Senate nominee. 8b5026abb99a.text: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro is an electoral juggernaut in America's biggest swing state — and he's widely seen as a likely contender for president in 2028. But strategists in both parties question how tested he really is. Shapiro's success — he's cruised to victory in multiple statewide races — has come with an asterisk: He hasn't faced a well-financed opponent in recent contests, leading some political insiders to see him as more of a wildcard than his resume suggests. Why it matters: Shapiro's unfamiliarity with intense, bruising campaigns could become a liability in the 2028 Democratic primary, where if he was a top candidate, he'd be confronted with a barrage of attack ads, opposition research and rivals with deep pockets. A plugged-in Democratic operative in Pennsylvania suggested that because of Shapiro's lack of being tested, "it is totally possible that he has an incredible glass jaw — and that he is the Scott Walker of 2028." Walker was the swing-state Wisconsin governor who looked good on paper as a potential presidential candidate but flopped after entering the 2016 GOP primary. Zoom in: In next week's election, Shapiro is running for a second four-year term as the Keystone State's governor. He's on pace to defeat Republican challenger Stacy Garrity by double digits, according to the latest polls. The money gap is gargantuan: Shapiro has dropped $42 million on campaign ads, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. Garrity, the state's treasurer, has spent just $3 million on ads — a drop in the ocean in a state as large as Pennsylvania, with its expensive advertising markets. It's not that Garrity prefers, say, door-knocking to TV ads. She's just outmatched: Campaign finance reports show she's only raised about $11 million this cycle, compared with Shapiro's $64 million. Making matters worse for Garrity, the Republican Governors Association (RGA) has not come to her rescue on the airwaves. Christopher Nicholas, a longtime GOP strategist in Pennsylvania, said the dynamic has "allowed Shapiro to skate with essentially having a one-sided campaign." "A lot of people think he has a glass chin because he's never really had a million dollars of negative TV shoved down his throat in a week," Nicholas said. Zoom out: Shapiro caught a break when he first ran for governor in 2022 against Republican Doug Mastriano , a far-right state senator widely viewed as a historically weak candidate disliked even by the GOP establishment. Mastriano, who was strapped for cash, spent just $2 million on ads that year. Shapiro and his allies spent $55 million. A conservative outside group invested $8 million on advertising in the election but abandoned the race that September after Shapiro embraced school vouchers, a priority for many on the right. The RGA stayed out of the race. In both of his gubernatorial contests , Shapiro has run unopposed in the Democratic primaries, leaving him little experience of intra-party electoral battles. It was a similar story when Shapiro twice was elected as Pennsylvania's attorney general. He vastly outspent his Republican opponents. What they're saying: Shapiro's allies argue that he's had token opposition precisely because he's a formidable candidate — that more talented Republicans don't want to waste their time and money running against such a hard-to-beat opponent with big fundraising chops. The governor has also sometimes cut off his GOP rivals' money spigots by courting Republican donors. "Sun Tzu was always about picking the battle you want to fight," said Doc Sweitzer, a Pennsylvania Democratic ad maker. "Josh has an incredible skill of picking the opponents." Asked for comment, Shapiro spokesperson Manuel Bonder said: "Winning elections in Pennsylvania and putting a check on Donald Trump is the only thing we're focused on — and believe it or not, it's harder than sitting at home giving unnamed quotes to Axios." Garrity spokesperson Matt Beynon responded: "No amount of money will heal the wounds Josh Shapiro's inflicted over the past four years, it's going to take new leadership." The other side: Shapiro is far from the only potential Democratic presidential candidate who hasn't squared off against a top-notch statewide Republican candidate. Possible White House hopefuls from deep-blue territory — such as New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, or with little experience defeating Republicans statewide, like former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, have either never run in or never won remotely competitive general elections. Flashback: Shapiro's critics make the case that regardless of why he hasn't been challenged much, he and his team haven't had to deal with reams of opposition research being dug up about him, or tens of millions of dollars in negative ads aired against him. One of the only times Shapiro came close to experiencing that was when he was under consideration to be former Vice President Kamala Harris' running mate in 2024 — and, they say, that didn't turn out well . Shapiro faced a mountain of tough press over topics on which he'd never faced significant scrutiny, such as a college op-ed piece in which he called Palestinians "too battle-minded" to exist peacefully with Israel. At the time, even some of Shapiro's closest supporters felt he didn't respond effectively to the negative articles.

a3790ebbff1a.text: By — Jovana Gec, Associated Press Jovana Gec, Associated Press By — Justin Spike, Associated Press Justin Spike, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/serbias-strongman-leader-vucic-concedes-defeat-to-student-led-movement-in-seismic-political-shift Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Serbia's strongman leader Vucic concedes defeat to student-led movement in seismic political shift World Updated on Oct 25, 2026 5:57 PM EDT — Published on Oct 25, 2026 5:35 PM EDT BELGRADE, Serbia (AP) — The long-serving strongman leader of Serbia, Aleksandar Vucic, conceded defeat on Sunday in an election that pitted him and his right-wing party against a diverse student-led opposition movement that spent two years protesting his government. It was a seismic political shift in the Balkan country where Vucic, who had been endorsed by Russian President Vladimir Putin and who denounced the student movement as a foreign-led attempt to unseat him, led with virtually absolute power for 14 years. READ MORE: Presidential race in Bulgaria heads to runoff due to record low turnout Almost immediately, crowds flooded the streets of the capital Belgrade and other Serbian cities in an outburst of euphoric celebration. High turnout and gathering tensions marked the highly contested parliamentary election that was a showdown between Vucic and his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party and university students who, accusing the government of corruption and dismantling democracy, had built a popular following across the country. Serbia's 6.4 million voters were electing lawmakers to the 250-member Parliament. In conceding the election, Vucic said his party projects that his opponents, the youth-backed Students' List, will take between 135 and 140 seats while his SNS party will have around 105. "The Students' List has won," Vucic told supporters at his party's election night event, though he blamed Serbia's independent media as well as alleged interference by unnamed European countries and an "American deep state" for the loss. Belgrade erupts in celebration Vucic said that his SNS party won around 1.7 million votes compared to the Students' List, which he said took around 2.2 million. Supporters of the Students' List drove around Belgrade in cars, honking horns, singing, shouting and chanting: "Aleksandar is gone," referring to Vucic. Crowds swiftly dismantled the fences and tents at a park in central Belgrade where Vucic's loyalists had been camping for over a year and gathered earlier on Sunday. The outcome, which Vucic announced only around an hour and a half after polls closed, came after tensions had built as voting progressed during the day. Police in anti-riot gear had cordoned off an area in central Belgrade around the election commission headquarters. Special police vehicles could be seen near the pro-Vucic camp, and large groups of black-clad men had congregated at various points throughout the city. Protests over corruption lead to Vucic's fall Ilija Srdanovic, first on the electoral list "Student List - Students Win", celebrates following the first results of the parliamentary election in Belgrade, Serbia, on Oct. 25, 2026. Photo by Djordje Kojadinovic/Reuters Vucic was seeking become Serbia's prime minister after serving two near-full terms as president. He resigned the presidency last month to lead the campaign. Support for the populist had eroded since 16 people were killed in 2024 when a concrete canopy collapsed at a train station in Novi Sad. That set off a wave of youth protests that blamed the collapse on high-level corruption, cronyism and rampant graft during renovation work at the station. Dijana Hrka, the mother of one of the victims, was in the crowd celebrating in Belgrade. Sobbing, Hrka told N1 television: "I have been waiting for this moment for two years." "Now I expect that they will all be held accountable," she said. Despite the protests, Vucic retained considerable support among many of Serbia's voters. Admirers viewed him as a capable leader who can steer the nation through global uncertainties — the image that was carefully crafted by the mainstream media. Student movement campaigned on rebuilding democracy While the increasingly authoritarian Vucic has routinely outplayed Serbia's fractured opposition in the past, the leaderless youth movement proved to be a tough opponent that rattled his firm grip on power in Serbia like no one else in the 14 years since his party took office. The newly formed Students' List movement was shaped by university students but none actually appeared on the election list. Instead, its candidates are little-known experts, athletes, farmers and artists. READ MORE: Iranians fear a possible return to all-out war as U.S. and Israeli elections approach This approach was meant to counter Vucic's one-man rule and restore a sense of community and solidarity. The students' message during the campaign focused on a non-partisan effort to rebuild Serbia's economy and restore its democracy. The students have used youthful energy to attract voters who are disillusioned with local politicians. Vilified by pro-government media, they cycled and walked through the country to reach voters in rural areas — Vucic's traditional strongholds. The student victory echoed the recent electoral defeat of a Vucic ally in Hungary, where youth participation helped oust the autocratic Viktor Orbán after 16 years and bring in a new pro-European government. It was likely to resonate beyond Serbia as countries across Europe have faced angry youth and student protests. The vote was closely watched in the EU Monitors predicted that total turnout in the election could reach around 70%, unseen in Serbia since 2000. During the day, long queues formed at polling stations in Serbia and in cities around the world. The globally-minded tech news startup Rest of World is scrambling to find a new home â or faces the prospect of shutting down.
The six-year-old digital publication has seen the social and web search traffic on which it depends evaporate. This sharp decline has prompted the organizationâs founder and primary financial backer, Sophie Schmidt, to explore other options for its future.
In recent months, Schmidt has held conversations with what one person familiar with the situation described as several large institutions about potentially absorbing Rest of World. But while conversations with potential partners are ongoing, the organization is also preparing for a grimmer outcome. Two people familiar with the plans told Semafor that the organization has selected a wind-down date for the publication in late January, a contingency intended to ensure employees receive exit packages and to give them a chance to look for new jobs if they so choose.
Schmidt wrote in an email to donors, in anticipation of this report, that Rest of World will âcease publishing as a standalone entityâ at the end of January, according to The New York Times.
Schmidt declined to comment. One person familiar with her thinking told Semafor that while Schmidt is proud of the organizationâs staff and journalism, she has privately conceded that the decline in audience has lessened Rest of Worldâs impact.
Rest of World launched in 2020 with an ambitious goal: to shift Western perspectives by telling global stories about technology often ignored by the mainstream US news outlets. A few months into its launch, Schmidt described the outlet as her âlifeâs project,â and told The Wall Street Journal that she would commit $60 million to it.
The outlet â initially organized as a nonprofit and funded at first largely by Schmidt, rather than advertising or subscriptions â hired dozens of journalists and built out a fast network of freelancers. Rest of World received some critical acclaim and broke several stories that prompted global policy changes, including its reporting on Uber Eats in South Africa and on mapping in rural Borneo.
But over the last 18 months, its fortunes began to shift.
Around the beginning of the second Trump administration, Rest of World saw a sharp decline in online web traffic, prompting concern from its leadership and a scramble to hold onto its audiences. The organization reprioritized Western readers in an attempt to sharpen its connection with the audience most likely to read its content, and chose to focus coverage on regions it believed remained true to its mission but would more easily appeal to American readers, like China. It began requiring visitors to register with the site in order to read articles.
None of the moves seemed to stop the publication from hemorrhaging readership.
Insiders cited broad industry-wide online traffic problems plaguing numerous online publishers, including Metaâs decision to deprioritize links to news articles and the rise of chatbots and AI summaries, which have decimated search traffic. It also wasnât positioned to take advantage of increases in media attention tied to Trump and US politics.
But the organizationâs leaders also attributed the decline to a deeper cultural shift to the right within the tech community. One senior leader at the organization said they believe tech news readers who previously expressed liberal values and an appetite for consuming global journalism have grown disillusioned with the news media, and now prefer an information diet of inward-looking podcasts, YouTube shows, and chatbot outputs.
Maxâs view
Rest of Worldâs audience struggles are not unique. Media companies that previously largely produced written content have found themselves scrambling to adapt to a world dominated by short- and long-form video consumption. Many have reacted by retreating, focusing on cultivating niche audiences.
Nowhere is this audience fragmentation clearer than in tech media, which is increasingly dominated by largely sycophantic media outlets owned by the decisionmakers themselves. A new generation of tech news consumers have turned their backs on the likes of Wired and The Verge in favor of self-congratulatory or friendly podcasts, newsletters, and X accounts.
Outlets like Rest of World, that rely on expensive-to-produce stories published somewhat infrequently, have struggled. It is, however, darkly ironic that the news organization launched by the scion of the former Google CEO has fallen victim to the changes Big Tech brought to the internet.

A relative outsider has been elected the new leader of the Canadian province of British Columbia after the provincial Conservatives swept to power in a snap election.
Lorne Doerkson, who took the helm of the party just weeks ago, will be British Columbia's new premier after the Conservatives won a majority of seats in the legislative assembly. It's the first time the party has won in the province in nearly a century.
Outgoing Premier David Eby, of the New Democratic Party (NDP), called the snap election last month - two years early - in an attempt to shore up power for his party.
Eby's gamble backfired in what has become the province's biggest political shakeup in decades.
A former rodeo announcer and newspaper publisher, Doerkson was first elected to the British Columbia (BC) Legislative Assembly in 2020.
But the 58-year-old was surprised himself when he found out, while on a flight home from South Africa last month, that his caucus colleagues wanted him as the party's new figurehead.
The news came shortly after the former leader of the BC Conservatives, Kerry-Lynne Findlay, resigned in September due to internal party conflict that saw a third of her caucus quit the party.
"Of course, it was a little bit of a short notice," Doerkson said in an interview with Canadian broadcaster CBC earlier this month.
Eby, who became premier in 2022, sought to take advantage of the divided BC Conservatives by calling the snap election.
He said the western Canadian province needed a "fire break" against US President Donald Trump's economic attacks and "Trump-style politics that threaten to infect" the province.
He defended his early election call by arguing his left-leaning party needed a bigger majority in the assembly to get its policies passed more quickly and easily.
"A one-seat majority meant every single vote could bring down the government," he said in a campaign video.
But Saturday's election results show voters were ready for someone new.
The NDP is projected to have won just 27 of the 93 total seats, while Doerkson's Conservatives are projected to have won 64.
The BC Green Party won two seats.
"British Columbians are hardworking, trailblasing people," Doerkson said in his victory speech Saturday night. "They want a fair shot at building something in this province."
That "trailblasing spirit", he said, "just needs government that's on its side."
Doerkson has promised to cut red tape "like it's never been cut before" by fast-tracking forestry and mining permits, and to triple natural gas production by 2035.
Eby resigned as provincial NDP leader in his concession speech, and said he accepts "full responsibility" for the outcome.
The provincial Conservative win comes after another recent shakeup in Canadian provincial politics when earlier this month, Quebec's sovereigntist Parti Quebecois won enough seats in the provincial election to form a minority government, adding a new test for Canada's unity.

10e506dcaa23.text: By — Alex Veiga, Associated Press Alex Veiga, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/home-sellers-are-lowering-their-prices-and-helping-buyers-to-make-a-deal-in-a-stagnant-market Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Home sellers are lowering their prices and helping buyers to make a deal in a stagnant market Economy Oct 25, 2026 4:55 PM EDT LOS ANGELES (AP) — Not long ago, a homeowner in America might reasonably wager they could sell their home fairly quickly, and for more than their asking price. That's unlikely to be a winning bet now. Across the nation, a stagnant housing market is leaving many sellers in limbo, unable to relocate for a new job, buy their next home to accommodate a growing family or follow through with other major life decisions that necessitate selling their home. WATCH: High mortgage rates compound housing affordability challenges Sellers who have the option to pull their listing off the market are generally doing so. Those who don't are under increased pressure to lower their asking price and also kick in thousands of dollars toward a buyer's costs, real estate agents say. The trend marks a stark turn from earlier this decade, when sellers often received well above their asking price as home shoppers empowered by rock-bottom mortgage rates fueled a buying frenzy that sent home prices soaring. Now, the market is stalled by surging mortgage rates, the compounding effect from years of rising home prices and an economic outlook dimmed by high inflation. Those factors are putting homeownership out of reach for many buyers while others delay a purchase and hope for more favorable conditions, perhaps in the spring. Sellers easily outnumber buyers and are stuck between uneasy choices: be more aggressive on price cuts and concessions to woo buyers, or hold out longer, even if it means delaying major life plans. "The dynamic has shifted back toward more of what we call buyers' markets rather than sellers' markets," said Mark Fleming, chief economist at First American Financial. "(That) means you might have to reduce your price, you might give a concession to get your home sold, it might have to stay on market longer." More than a year after first listing her home, an empty nester can move on With her three kids no longer living at home, Liz Suder decided to sell her four-bedroom, 3.5-bath house in Murphy, Texas, about 20 miles outside of Dallas, and buy a smaller place. "I was waiting to sell the house before I started looking," said Suder, 56. "I didn't want to have two mortgages." Suder wound up putting her life on hold for more than a year. The finance director, who owned the home for 21 years, initially put the house on the market in April 2025 for $750,000. Six months later, despite lowering the price several times, the home still hadn't sold and she took it off the market. Suder relisted the home in February for $725,000 ahead of the spring homebuying season. But it wasn't until recently that a home shopper agreed to buy it for $650,000. Suder sweetened the deal by kicking in $9,000 toward repairs. "I never expected it to take a full year, and for me to have to reduce the price by that much," she said. Life on hold, but holding the line on a major price cut Rick Ganga needs to find a buyer for his home in the coastal city of Blaine, Washington, before he can begin the next chapter in his life. Ganga is going through a divorce that requires the home to be sold. He's had multiple showings of the three-bedroom, 2.5-bath house since it went on the market on June 1 for $825,000. Lowering the price to just under $800,000 hasn't helped. "There's (been) no offers, virtually zero traffic," said Ganga, 58. READ MORE: Almost nowhere in California is building enough housing. Here's why Ganga said some sellers in his neighborhood have dropped their asking price by $100,000 or more, but because he's only owned the home since 2022, he hasn't built up enough equity to be able to lower the price any further. "That's not anything I'm going to entertain," he said. "It doesn't make sense." Until the home sells, the operations manager has little choice but to set aside plans to transfer with his company to another state. "I honestly believe that it will probably sit until spring or summer of next year," he said. Sellers losing leverage as the housing market stalls After briefly dipping below 6% in February, the average rate on a 30-year mortgage surged as high as 7.4% this month, its highest level in nearly three years. The upward march in rates has stifled U.S. home sales. With many sellers lowering their asking price, the national median home listing price declined in September from a year earlier for the 11th month in a row, dropping 1.2% to $419,250, according to Realtor.com. All told, about 21% of listings in September had their initial price lowered, a four-year high. It's not unusual for home shoppers to ask for — and receive — money from sellers to put toward their closing costs. Higher mortgage rates are also giving buyers leverage to press sellers for money to buy down their rate for a few years or for the life of the loan, reducing their overall borrowing costs. WATCH: What's in the housing affordability bill that Trump refused to sign "It's sort of like an indicator of where the market is right now, with buyers gaining leverage at the expense of sellers, and sellers doing more now to meet buyers halfway," said Jake Krimmel, a senior economist at Realtor.com. That's good news for home shoppers, but may not be enough to overcome the affordability hurdles keeping many prospective homebuyers out of the market. Consider, last month there were about 63% more sellers than homebuyers across the 50 largest U.S. metropolitan areas, according to an analysis by Redfin. And the number of buyers — roughly 929,000 — represented the fewest on record dating back to 2013, while the tally of sellers jumped to its highest

49134767dd3a.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/presidential-race-in-bulgaria-heads-to-runoff-due-to-record-low-turnout Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Presidential race in Bulgaria heads to runoff due to record low turnout World Oct 25, 2026 4:39 PM EDT SOFIA, Bulgaria (AP) — The presidential election in Bulgaria on Sunday ended inconclusively, with the next head of state to be picked in a runoff, according to election officials. A record low turnout, attributed by observers to a general mistrust in politicians resulting in voter apathy, will pit two contrasting political visions against each other in a highly polarized contest on Nov. 1. In a surprisingly strong performance, the candidate of the pro-Western reformist opposition, Andrey Gyurov, will face the incumbent leftist president, Iliana Yotova, setting clear lines of division regarding the country's future relationships with other nations. READ MORE: Iranians fear a possible return to all-out war as U.S. and Israeli elections approach Bulgarians voted against a backdrop of growing economic hardship and drone attacks on Black Sea shipping. The vote is the first major test for the Moscow-friendly Progressive Bulgaria party of Prime Minister Rumen Radev after its triumph in parliamentary elections in April. Despite a record number of candidates, the race had been expected to be decided in a runoff between incumbent Yotova, backed by Radev's party, and former caretaker Prime Minister Gyurov, who is backed by pro-Western opposition parties. The campaign focused heavily on Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the widening hostilities in the Black Sea, where recent drone attacks on commercial vessels off Bulgaria's coast have heightened security concerns in the European Union and NATO member country. The strikes have raised concerns over Russia's intentions to escalate the conflict and prompted the government to ask Bulgaria's partners for assistance to strengthen its maritime security. Candidates also sought to address public anxiety over rising energy prices and inflation, as many families, particularly in rural areas, struggle to make ends meet. The election had been expected to go to a runoff as none of the 27 candidates was expected to win outright. Turnout must be above 50% of 6.6 million registered voters, and the winner needs a majority of votes. Bulgaria's incumbent president is a front-runner Yotova, a 62-year-old journalist and former member of the European Parliament, is the country's incumbent president and a front-runner in the race. She previously served as vice president under Radev, during his two terms as head of state. She took over the presidency in January 2026, when Radev stepped down to run for parliament, and is now seeking her own mandate. She's running as an independent but also has the official backing of Progressive Bulgaria and the Socialist Party, where her career began. If she wins, Yotova will become Bulgaria's first elected female president. READ MORE: Former president Rumen Radev will win Bulgaria election, exit poll suggests Analysts expect her to continue Radev's policy to keep Bulgaria on its European path but at the same time call for improved relations with Russia and the lifting of sanctions. Both Yotova and Radev have called for a diplomatic solution to end the war in Ukraine. Addressing supporters at a rally this week, Yotova said she "advocated for peace through negotiations, rather than force." Observers say that Yotova's victory would keep the presidency in the hands of the ruling majority, and such concentration of power could prevent institutions maintaining effective checks and balances on policy decisions. A former deputy central bank governor is the main challenger in the race Yotova's main challenger is economist Andrei Gyurov, a former deputy governor of the central bank and caretaker prime minister who led the country in the early months of 2026. He is supported by the pro-Western reformist opposition. Gyurov, who has often expressed firm support for Ukraine, signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his premiership. "I want Bulgaria to have a voice of its own in Europe. A reliable NATO ally that defends its interests through preparedness, strong diplomacy and a clear position," he told supporters this week. Exit poll results show Yotova with 3% to 4% ahead of Gyurov. Presidents in Bulgaria are elected directly for a five-year term and can serve no more than two terms. While the post is primarily ceremonial, the direct election gives the president greater political authority. The president leads the armed forces and can veto legislation, signs international treaties and appoints ambassadors. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. c0ee3ffdcfef.text: By — Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/judge-asked-to-compel-trump-administration-to-disclose-emails-and-texts-about-kennedy-center-plans Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge asked to compel Trump administration to disclose emails and texts about Kennedy Center plans Politics Oct 25, 2026 3:49 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's administration is withholding records documenting the scope of his influence over management of the Kennedy Center, according to attorneys for a Democratic lawmaker challenging the Republican president's plan to close the performing arts center for renovations. A list of records in the Kennedy Center's possession suggests that Trump has been in "near-constant contact" with the center's management, either directly or through intermediaries, plaintiffs' lawyers said in a court filing on Sunday. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Attorneys for Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and ex officio member of the Kennedy Center board, are seeking a court order for the administration to turn over documents, emails and text messages that it has withheld based on its claims that they contain privileged presidential communications. "These communications directly bear on the issues before the Court, and the claim of privilege cannot stand," Beatty's lawyers wrote. U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper didn't immediately rule on their request to compel disclosure of the records. READ MORE: Kennedy Center Honors to be held at Capital One Arena amid fight over adding Trump's name The list of withheld documents includes 19 text messages between Kennedy Center executive director and CEO Matt Floca and Trump executive assistant Natalie Harp regarding Kennedy Center-related matters. They exchanged 11 of those messages on Sept. 15, when the center's board voted for a third time to close the facility, according to Beatty's lawyers. The list also includes approximately 180 center-related texts between Floca and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who was acting as Trump's "go-between," Beatty's lawyers say. The plaintiffs' attorneys suspect the administration is engaging in impermissible "gamesmanship." "Without access to these materials, (Beatty) will lack a complete picture of Defendants' actions," they wrote. The White House didn't immediately comment on the court filing. Cooper, who was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Barack Obama, ruled in May that the Kennedy Center illegally added Trump's name to the building and ordered it removed. Trump, who was named the Kennedy Center's chairman last year by loyalists on its board, has said the building is in dangerous condition that will require it to be "ripped down." The board voted to close the center after Cooper blocked the institution from returning Trump's name to the building. On Sept. 16, Floca ordered a temporary closure of the center's main building. A day later, Cooper ordered the Kennedy Center to provide 30 days' notice before making any major physical changes to the building. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 6c8174c3d48e.text: Brazil President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was elected to a fourth, nonconsecutive term in the nation's presidential election according to early results released Sunday evening. Why it matters: Lula's victory deals a setback to Brazil's right-wing populist movement and preserves a major counterweight to President Trump 's influence in Latin America, with tensions over trade and tariffs threatening to persist. Lula, the incumbent candidate, was facing Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro . Flávio was widely seen as the heir to the nation's right-wing populist movement. The big picture: The election has been shaped by the impact of U.S. tariffs, climate change and the Amazon rainforest, 60% of which is in Brazil. Bolsonaro campaigned on public security and tackling corruption, presenting himself as a continuation of his father's political legacy, while Lula emphasized defending Brazilian sovereignty against U.S. pressure. Yet substantive policy debate was limited, with both candidates focusing instead on corruption allegations levied against the opposing camp, wrote Matthew Taylor, a Brazil politics expert at American University. Zoom in: After the U.S. imposed additional 25% tariffs on some Brazilian goods this summer, Lula accused Bolsonaro of being "Trump's candidate" and the U.S. president of wanting to "colonize" Brazil. Lula has enacted climate policies aimed at reversing environmental deregulation under the previous administration, while Bolsonaro denied climate change and pledged to continue his father's political legacy. Amazon deforestation has fallen 71% since 2022, the year before Lula returned to office, reaching its lowest annual level on record in 2026. Yet Lula's environmental record is complicated by his support for expanded oil development. Lula defeated Jair Bolsonaro in the previous election. The elder Bolsonaro is now serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup to overturn the 2022 election, though he remains under house arrest due to health problems.

- Published
George McMaster's farming career started with milking eight cows in a byre, relying on his eyes to spot any health issues in his cattle.
He still watches his now-300-strong herd, but via a feed from an AI camera in the milking parlour at the farm near Islandmagee in County Antrim.
The device uses an algorithm which assigns each cow its own ID, records a short video of the animal every day, analyses it and flags any changes - often before they are visible to the human eye.
For the third generation farmer, it is "absolutely incredible to move from all hand-done to sitting on the phone, watching what's happening outside".
Making everyone happy
It is just one example of how technology is changing the traditional profession.
George's son Jack, who is taking over the farm, jumped at the chance to get involved with the CattleEye app when a local developer approached him.
He, too, is astonished by the potential.
"There's cows there we would never have thought of as lame when we were just watching them every day, but whenever the camera's watching they're picking them up so much earlier, any emergencies that we have, to check cows before they lose condition and get sick," he said.
"And if cows are in better health, we get more milk and they're happier - happy cows make happy farmers."
Simplifying business
Caleb Howard is using technology to manage his 90 Jersey cows on the farm near Coagh in County Tyrone.
They filter in and out of a robotic milking machine when they want to, rather than being herded in at set times.
Like the McMasters, he thinks "everything is going down the robotic route" to improve efficiency.
But historically in a place like rural Tyrone, that has come with its own challenges.
Getting high-speed broadband was a game-changer for him - he has been able to open a farm shop with an electronic payment system.
"Ten years ago, in our area, phone signal was rubbish, the broadband wasn't great, it was just like a slightly faster dial-up," he said.
"So now everything is much simpler and much easier-used when you've got a good internet connection."
Project Stratum was set up to deliver high-speed broadband to areas like the one Howard lives in.
Colin Hutchinson from Fibrus, which delivered the project, said it had had a "massive" economic impact.
"Being online and having good broadband access is really crucial now," he said.
"And it's enabling businesses like this to thrive in really rural locations."
'Facebook for cows'
Robert Smyth runs a herd of 100 dairy cows in another rural location, near Randalstown in County Antrim.
For four years now, he has used the FarmDrive app to run the business.
"It's so much handier - beforehand you're writing things down, bits of paperwork in the cattle house and writing them down in the office, whereas now you just do it at that time," he said.
"And then whenever you have inspections coming up, all you have to do is go into your compliance section, select reports, and there's your reports for your medicine, for your meal records, for everything.
"The AI really should be looking towards how to manage your farm better and how to reduce your inputs and increase your outputs."
Developer Gareth McDonald describes FarmDrive as "Facebook for cows". Each animal gets a profile with all her records in one place and a photo can be added.
He comes from a farming background and studied computer science.
Although he is passionate about the technology, he does not believe it will replace humans.
"It's allowing us to work a lot more quickly and efficiently, and on the farming side, it's basically allowing the farmer to see the right information at the right time, where it's kind of that adviser to the farmer," he said.
"We're very much of the opinion we don't want the AI making the decision for the farmer."
Data-driven industry
Almost a century ago, County Down-born inventor Harry Ferguson transformed the farming industry when he developed the linkage system still used in tractors today.
Former president of the Ulster Farmers' Union Ian Marshall says AI is similarly revolutionary.
While the industry has always relied on data, he believes technology will drive how information is used.
"When we take all the datasets, then I think we can deliver on the three pillars of sustainability - economic, environmental and social," he said.
"So I think that because we've got so much data and so much digitalisation in the industry, that farmers will certainly use this to their advantage and can meet their targets, meet their objectives and meet the obligations whilst delivering good quality, sustainable food."

Rapper Nicki Minaj said US President Donald Trump has "changed the energy of the country" as she joined him at a Michigan rally to stump for Republicans ahead of the nationwide midterm elections.
"He's given us a future to look forward to," she said, after Trump praised her figure and called her on stage to speak.
Minaj has called herself Trump's "number one fan" despite criticising some of his policies in his first term.
In Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is locked in a tight race with Republican Mike Rogers with just over a week to go before the midterms. Former President Barack Obama held a rally - one of the first in this cycle - with the Democrat on Saturday.
Democrats are also aggressively hitting the campaign trail, with close elections taking place on 3 November which will decide which party controls Congress for the rest of Trump's presidency.
In his remarks on Sunday, Trump focused on El-Sayed's Muslim faith and background, alleging that he will "invite jihadists" into America if he wins.
El-Sayed has criticised similar remarks by Trump as Islamophobic, saying in an ad to voters last week that the US president "thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor's office".
In Port Huron on Sunday, Minaj, wearing a gold-coloured Gucci-branded suit, led the crowd in chanting Trump's name, and the names of Republican candidates in Michigan.
"We really need all these great people to be elected, because this is a major turning point for our country," she said.
"She never looked more beautiful," Trump said as she left the stage. "She gets it. She's smart," he added.
Earlier in his speech, Trump praised the rear end of one male Republican candidate before turning the crowd's attention to Minaj.
"By the way, I looked at a beautiful ass before," he segued. "Nicki Minaj. That's hard to miss."
He then asked her to "stand up" as the crowd cheered, and added that he hoped she was not "insulted" by his remark.
The Super Bass singer had accompanied Trump to the state aboard Air Force One. She filmed a video with an aide - which was posted to X -on the president's plane, pretending to be interviewing for the White House press secretary role.
The position is currently open after Katie Zacharia left five days after a shaky public debut.
The Trinidad and Tobago-born rapper has thrown her star power behind Trump a few times before, including on his allegations that Christians face persecution in Nigeria and his "gold card" visa, which offers applicants residency and a path to US citizenship.

The partner set to take over leadership of Weil, Gotshal & Manges has held talks to leave the firm for a rival, a move that would compound ongoing talent drain at one of Wall Streetâs top dealmaking and restructuring shops.
Ramona Nee, Weilâs co-managing partner, has had discussions to join Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, according to people familiar with the matter. Nee, an adviser to big private equity firms including Advent, was slated to take over as Weilâs sole chair in January.
Weil declined to comment. Nee did not return a request for comment. Her departure is not guaranteed and the talks could fall apart, the people said.
If she does leave, she would follow a flood of Weilâs top talent out the door and the breakdown of merger talks with crosstown rival Willkie Farr & Gallagher. Rainmaker Michael Aiello defected to Cravath, Swaine & Moore with a team of partners. It would be likely that a sizable portion of Weilâs Boston partnership would leave with her, according to one person familiar with the matter who is close with many of Weilâs top Boston lawyers.
Nee had told Weil partners she would not take the chair job, which was announced last spring, according to a person briefed on the communication. The Financial Times earlier reported that decision.
Remaining and former Weil lawyers place blame on Aielloâs departure â and Neeâs possible departure â at the feet of executive partner Barry Wolf, who has helmed the firm to some success for more than a decade but in recent years has failed to convince senior partners that Weil has a vision for a world where AI and outsize pay packages upend the perceived usefulness of high-end legal advice.
Aielloâs departure came as a result, in part, because top Weil leaders including Wolf failed to lay out a convincing long-term vision for the firm, according to a person familiar with his thinking.

8cac775fae01.text: A student-led protest movement has ended the 14-year rule of Serbia's right-wing party, former President Aleksandar Vučić conceded Sunday. Why it matters: The historic upset sidelines a Balkan strongman who courted President Trump's family and allies, raising questions about future U.S. relations with a country that has balanced ties with Russia and the West. Vučić 's outreach has included the president's son Donald Trump Jr. and longtime ally Richard Grenell, while a proposed development involving Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner became embroiled in controversy. The big picture: The movement's electoral breakthrough reflects a broader wave of youth activism in Europe, where young people have mobilized over corruption, education and economic pressures. The victory could usher in democratic reforms in Serbia, where Vučić consolidated power. Driving the news: Vučić said Sunday evening it was "clear" that his Serbian Progressive Party had lost to the student-backed electoral movement, although official results had yet to be announced, according to translations of his announcement . He projected the Student List would win between 135 and 140 seats in the 250-seat parliament, compared with 105 for his coalition. Cardiologist Ilija Srdanović heads the Student List, though the grassroots movement emphasized its decentralized leadership. The result echoes the student-led movement that helped topple Slobodan Milošević in 2000 , with Serbians reviving that era's "He's finished!" rallying cry as they celebrated Sunday. Context: The movement emerged from mass protests after the November 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad that killed 16 people, fueling public anger over alleged government corruption. It subsequently evolved into an electoral movement campaigning for accountability and institutional reform. What's next: The Student List must choose a prime minister and form a government while Serbia faces a separate presidential election in December to replace Vučić.

A software developer became so frustrated by the amount of rubbish he saw dumped along roadsides that he built an AI-powered "litter dashcam" to expose the scale of the problem.
Robin Bennett, from Shrewsbury, developed the Roadside Litter app after noticing what he believed was a growing amount of litter while driving around the county.
The technology has already logged more than 3,000 litter reports in Shropshire and more than 28,000 across the UK.
He is now sharing the data with anti-litter campaign group Clean Up Britain in the hope it will encourage action, while Shropshire Council said it was exploring ways to improve litter management on some of the county's busiest roads.
Bennett, who runs a software company in Telford, said he found the amount of rubbish on local roads "really depressing" and wanted to understand whether the issue was unique to Shropshire or part of a wider national problem.
After approaching Clean Up Britain to ask how he could help, he went on to develop what he describes as a "litter dashcam" that records rubbish spotted from a vehicle.
"My software company's created an app, which essentially is a litter dashcam," he said.
"The app records the litter that it sees."
Mounted on a vehicle dashboard, the app automatically takes a photograph every 10 seconds, identifying visible litter and grading it against a national standard before uploading the information.
Bennett said: "I've got a phone holder stuck to the dashboard, I've put my phone in securely.
"I start it and that's it, you don't have to touch the screen, and the screen will go black in a minute so it's not distracting in any way.
"Every 10 seconds it takes a photo, it looks at the litter it can see by the side of the road and it grades it according to a national standard."
The app had recorded more than 3,000 reports in Shropshire and more than 28,000 nationwide, Bennett said.
He added litter was particularly common near convenience stores, fast-food outlets and motorway service stations.
"People pick up a bag of fast food and just throw the bag out the window," he added.
Bennett said he hoped the data collected by the app would help build a clearer picture of the problem and encourage authorities to do more to tackle roadside litter.
A spokesperson for Shropshire Council said the authority recognised the importance of maintaining a clean and attractive highway network and was engaging with National Highways to explore opportunities to improve litter management on the A5 and A49.

A discarded microwave, a mattress sodden by the rain and even a pile of used syringes. The reality of illegally dumped waste sits before me in a colossal mound next to the side of a motorway.
For the team I'm with, this is a jigsaw waiting to be pieced together and solved as they try to identify the criminal culprits.
It does not take long for Anthony Horan and Ashley Hanley from North East Lincolnshire Council to find answers within the mountain of waste on the side of the Brocklesby Interchange near Grimsby.
They tell me it is a goldmine of clues.
"I'm gobsmacked at the amount of evidence in this one," Anthony Horan, who works as a senior environmental health practitioner for the authority.
"I'm disgusted at the needles. I've never found this amount ever."
A number of times during the interview we pause after spotting a syringe close to our feet. Some are hidden under items, others are in plain sight.
About 20 are collected to be destroyed.
The team tells me this is exactly why they wear protective equipment.
Meanwhile, a picture starts to emerge as letters with different names and addresses - all miles outside the area - are fished out and photographed.
Horan tells me if evidence which identifies a person is found, they will be questioned.
If found liable, they could be fined if they have not properly undergone a "domestic duty of care".
"A lot of people think enviro-crime or fly-tipping is a victimless crime," Horan says. "It's not, there's many victims."
Horan says people often employ a "man with a van" to dispose of their waste, but frequently the person hired just dumps it.
If the waste is found dumped on private land, the owner will have to pay for its removal. Councils only pay if it is on public land.
Wearing thick gloves, environmental enforcement officer Hanley continues to dig through the dump.
I ask him about rogue waste removers and his advice for people wanting to get rid of waste.
"I would advise people to take the right precautions, make sure that they're giving it to somebody who has a waste carriage licence," Hanley says.
"Make sure that you're taking it to a proper waste facility if you're doing it yourself," he adds.
The Environment Agency says waste criminals "scar our environment and communities".
It says: "Illegal waste dumping is a crime that costs the public purse Â£1bn a year. We know the challenges and are working hard to overcome them."
It encourages the public to report suspected waste crime to its incident hotline or via its website.
In August, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said fines for fly-tipping would increase from Â£300 to Â£5,000 and offenders could be given up to nine points on their driving licence.
Across the Humber Bridge, I meet Hull City Council's Streetscene team as they arrive at a fly-tip in the middle of a housing estate.
Under this authority, the fines for fly-tipping are higher at Â£1,000.
As teams drag mattresses and wooden planks onto the truck, they tell a similarly frustrated story.
"It's all over the city and now it's on the rise," says Mike, one of the men clearing the waste.
"We've got a job to do so we have to clear it and move on to the next fly-tip and do the same again."
Carl Wilson, the team manager, tells me this location is a hotspot and criminals will be back soon enough.
"This will all get cleared away and then in a couple of weeks they'll probably do it again," Carl says.
"That's why you need this evidence to catch them, to stop them, to put it to a stop."
The authority tells me they often visit hotspots to deliver letters to residents on how to properly dispose of waste to prevent fly-tipping.
Back near Grimsby, I ask the North East Lincolnshire team what their message is to fly-tippers or people considering dumping their waste.
Horan is stern.
"Don't do it because we'll catch you," he says. "We don't want to be doing this, we want you to do the correct thing."
Additional reporting by Alice Toon

On 19 July about 18 tonnes of plastic nurdles, consisting of about one billion tiny balls, spilled into the River Tyne after a crash between ships at the Port of Tyne.
It is believed to be the worst recorded incident of its type in Europe.
In the months since, teams of volunteers have joined in efforts to collect the microplastics that continue to wash up on north-east England's coast.
But several questions remain. So what do we know about the spill right now - and what are we still waiting to find out?
What actually happened on 19 July?
A wind turbine installation vessel called the Wind Orca collided with a container ship berthed at the Port of Tyne.
A gantry crane on the quayside collapsed and ended up lying across the ship.
Two containers on the BG Orange were full of nurdles. These are pre-production plastic pellets, about the size of a lentil, which are used as the raw material to manufacture nearly all everyday plastic goods.
About 18 tonnes of these pellets spilled into the water because of the crash.
Who was at fault?
This is still being investigated.
Northumbria Police said it was investigating the collision and so far, no-one has been arrested. The Marine Accident Investigation Branch is also investigating.
The Port of Tyne previously said it, along with others, had asked the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) to consider enforcing safer transportation methods for nurdles, something environmental groups have long called for.
How much of the nurdles can actually be recovered?
By the end of September about 28% of the nurdles had been recovered, according to scientists.
But the Port of Tyne, the Environment Agency and the North East Mayoral Strategic Authority (MSA) said the numbers of nurdles washing up ashore had already "reduced significantly" by then and numbers were continuing to fall.
They said they believed the full recovery of the 18 tonnes was not achievable. When asked what percentage recovery rate would be considered a success, the bodies said they would measure success via various metrics including shoreline surveys.
Where will the nurdles go?
The pellets from the spill have been found along the English coast from Northumberland to North Yorkshire.
On Friday the Danish Environment Protection Agency confirmed pellets found on the country's western coast had also likely originated from the Tyne spill.
Dr Matthew Perks at Newcastle University and his colleagues are monitoring the movement of the nurdles and examining how the pellets may deteriorate in water.
The team's modelling so far suggests about one in eight of the billion nurdles remain in the Tyne estuary and high river flows could flush these microplastics downstream in the autumn.
Perks said this was a crucial opportunity to collect the pellets.
Nevertheless he said it was unclear how far some of the nurdles could really travel.
"As time goes by, it becomes more difficult to pinpoint the areas where these nodules are likely to be," he said.
It is also unclear when the nurdles will start breaking down into nanoplastics. "That will change the way they behave," he said.
What is the impact on wildlife?
Long story short â we do not know yet.
Professor Bhavani Narayanaswamy at the Scottish Association for Marine Science said it could be months or years before we understood the full impact of the spill.
She said the nurdles could affect wildlife in various ways, including getting stuck in animal digestive tracts and adsorbing chemicals which then may be toxic to wildlife when ingested.
Prof Narayanaswamy said there was little research on the long-term impact of plastic pollution on animals compared with its immediate effects.
Dan Turner, who coordinates the North East England Beached Bird Survey, said the group had collected several dead birds along the coast which they would be testing for nurdles next month.
"It is quite possible that the seabirds have mistaken the plastic for fish eggs," he previously told the BBC.
Who is paying for the clean-up?
Recovery is largely being paid for by insurers representing BG Orange, which was carrying the pellets, as well as local councils and the Port of Tyne.
Thousands of volunteers have also been involved in the clean-up.
Councils have been told to record their costs so they can seek compensation from the insurers of those ultimately found responsible.
And how long will it last for?
The multi-agency group, consisting of the North East MSA, Port of Tyne and the EA, said the nurdle recovery programme was continuing but it had increasingly moved away from "large-scale clean-up activity" towards "targeted recovery and monitoring".
Environmental charity Fidra said it was unclear how long the clean-up would need to continue, considering the fact that nurdles could stay in water for years.
It said a long-term plan was required to tackle the pollution and the plans should be "adequately resourced" with responsibility clearly defined.
Is it still worth going to beach cleans?
Volunteer Lou Shackleton said there was still a core group of individuals who gave up their spare time to monitor and recover nurdles on local beach.
She said the group needed all the help they could get.
"If you're happy to wrap up against the rain and the wind... come and join us," she said.

- Published
A convicted murderer serving a life sentence in Australia has lost his bid to overturn a ban on prisoners consuming Vegemite - the salty yeast-based spread that has become a national symbol.
Andre McKechnie argued that the ban, in place since 2006, denied him the right to "enjoy his culture as an Australian".
Authorities in the state of Victoria say inmates may use the strong-smelling paste to disguise contraband substances or to brew alcohol behind bars.
And on Monday, a Supreme Court judge rejected McKechnie's appeal, saying the prisoner's "cultural rights are limited primarily by the fact he has been sentenced to a term of imprisonment".
In his lawsuit against Victoria's Department of Justice and Corrections, the agency which manages the state's prisons, McKechnie, 54, said the ban on the spread breached law requiring prisons to provide food that allowed inmates to maintain their health and well-being but the judge said that had not been proven.
McKechnie was handed a life sentence for stabbing a property developer to death in Queensland in the 1990s. He served part of his sentence in Queensland before being transferred to Victoria.
During the hearing, the court heard evidence from Corrections Victoria that the smell of vegemite can distract sniffer dogs trying to detect drugs being brought into prison.
The product is also banned in jails in Queensland, South Australia and Tasmania.
A much-loved breakfast spread for some, Vegemite has acquired controversial accolades since it first hit shop shelves in Australia in 1923.
The thick, brown spread was invented in the Victorian capital of Melbourne more than a century ago as an alternative to the British spread Marmite.
It sparked an international dispute in April last year when an Australian cafe owner in Canada was told to remove jars of the condiment from his shelves as it did not comply with local health regulations.
Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese intervened in the row, saying it was "rather odd" that Canada allowed the sale of Vegemite's "rubbish" rival product Marmite. The cafe owner was later allowed to continue selling the spread.

The Scoop
The New York Times article appeared on September 24, 2025, under the headline The Billionaire, the Psychedelics and the Best-Selling Memoir.
The 4,980-word investigation by Katherine Rosman and Elisabeth Egan captured a wave of discomfort that had rippled from New Yorkâs publishing world to Amarillo, Texasâ police department about a bestselling memoir by a billionaire pillar of Manhattan society. Amy Griffinâs The Tell told the story of a woman whose perfect exterior masked childhood trauma, and how the drug MDMA helped her remember and ultimately move past childhood sexual abuse.
The Times story turned her success into a parable about class and Americaâs new ultrarich. Most damagingly, the Times discussed the possibility that Griffinâs memory of sexual abuse might have been borrowed from a classmate who attested that stories in The Tell were âeerily similar to the abuse she herself enduredâ in middle school from a different teacher.
Some of Griffinâs friends suggested she shrug off the bad press. But she was livid, consumed by it, friends said. It was intensely personal: In the days after the story, there had even been an exchange of Snap messages between Rosmanâs son, a student at the University of Southern California, and a friend of one of Griffinâs children. The messages, reviewed by Semafor, were heated but respectful.
The weekend after the story published, Griffin and her husband John Griffin, whose hedge fund was the source of their billions, were in the safe space of the superagent Ari Emanuelâs annual Aspen retreat, âThe Weekend.â A person seated with Griffin in Aspen recalled her saying the Times had sought to destroy her life and her familyâs.
Then Griffin said something that shocked her interlocutor, the person recalled: By calling into question Griffinâs account, Rosman had made her and her childrenâs life miserable â and she would do the same to the Times reporterâs son.
Griffin, through a spokesperson, heatedly disputed the claim: âAmy Griffin has never threatened Katherine Rosmanâs children or taken any action to harm Ms. Rosman or her family. These allegations are categorically false,â the spokesperson said.
The spokesperson cited the exchange of Snap messages after the story published. âAt an event shortly after publication, Mrs. Griffin was upset about the impact on her daughter and expressed those feelings in a conversation with a friend. Her words were later taken out of context and mischaracterized as a threat she never made.â
The person who heard Griffinâs comments in Aspen understood them as a threat, and said they felt obliged to act.
The person asked a mutual contact to warn Rosman, according to three people familiar with that exchange.
Rosman, in turn, alerted her employer. Then The New York Timesâ general counsel, David McCraw, spoke to Griffinâs lawyer, Tom Clare, though the two men offered somewhat different versions of what was said.
Thereâs no indication Griffin ever took any action against Rosmanâs son.
But Griffinâs focus on the Times story and other fallout has, acquaintances say, continued. The classmate, Joleene Altum, sued Griffin for emotional distress and invasion of privacy, and Griffin countersued for defamation in a bitter, ongoing legal battle. Itâs been covered breathlessly on Instagram and by celebrity media â led by the former Access Hollywood host Billy Bush, who last Monday on his podcast described being confronted by Griffin at a wedding on the Hawaiian island of Lanai.
