dfe23806c9d2.text: By — Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/brazils-flavio-bolsonaro-leaves-brazil-for-the-united-states-after-presidential-loss-according-to-multiple-media-reports Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Brazil's Flávio Bolsonaro leaves Brazil for the United States after presidential loss, according to multiple media reports World Oct 27, 2026 3:44 PM EDT SAO PAULO (AP) — Defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro has left Brazil for the United States following a stunning loss to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday's election, according to multiple media reports. A spokesperson for Bolsonaro did not respond to a request for comment. Bolsonaro's brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who lives in Texas, had publicly encouraged him to leave Brazil if he lost the election. WATCH: Lula prevails in Brazil but Flávio Bolsonaro refuses to concede Bolsonaro has touted his relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump and visited the White House in May. The family connections go deeper: His brother Eduardo Bolsonaro was convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration and sentenced to four years in prison. A warrant was recently issued for his arrest. While Trump did not offer a full-throated endorsement of Bolsonaro, as he has with some other right-of-center candidates in Latin America, he suggested on Monday, without providing evidence, that Brazil's election was "rigged." Bolsonaro's decision to leave Brazil came as a deadline for him to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports expired at noon Tuesday. It remained unclear whether he had complied. Bolsonaro, 45, was served with the order to surrender his passports Monday, a day after his stunning loss to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro said he received it outside the home where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula. The sealed Supreme Court order, viewed by The Associated Press, was issued Sunday. Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat and has made unsubstantiated allegations of election fraud. Bolsonaro initially asked for the election results to be annulled after an evening of chaos at some polling places that prompted authorities to extend voting by two hours. On Monday, he urged the electoral court to investigate alleged election fraud and nullify Lula's and Vice President Geraldo Alckmin's candidacies, which the electoral court has never done before. To overturn the result, Bolsonaro would have to present evidence of fraud affecting Lula's 4.4 million-vote margin and convince the eight-member electoral court before the results are certified on Dec. 18. Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, received more than 64 million votes, compared with fewer than 60 million for Bolsonaro, a margin of nearly 4%. Bolsonaro said in a video posted Monday on his social media channels that he had no plans to leave Brazil and instead was attempting to organize opposition among his congressional colleagues to the election results. His eight-year term as a senator expires Jan. 31, 2027, which will also cause him to lose special jurisdiction at the country's Supreme Court. Bolsonaro is under investigation by Brazil's Supreme Court for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in two cases. In one, he's accused of using a sports betting company to launder fraudulent deductions from government pensions paid to senior citizens. In the other, he is accused of accepting millions of dollars from a disgraced banker. He has denied any wrongdoing in both cases. Prosecutors suspect the funds from the banker were used to pay his brother Eduardo Bolsonaro's expenses and to promote Flávio Bolsonaro's political agenda with the Trump administration, documents show. Brazilians had earlier taken to social media to ask where Bolsonaro was. Reporters gathered outside his home in the capital, Brasilia, but he did not appear. A spokesperson for the Ministry of Security of Argentina denied reports the Brazilian senator had entered the country. Brazilian media outlets reported that many Bolsonaro allies had been unable to reach him. Paulo Figueiredo, a close ally of Bolsonaro's who lives in the United States, was asked about the senator's whereabouts and did not answer directly. "At this moment — following months of intense work that were unfairly thwarted — I have no desire to speak with the press. I kindly ask that you do not persist. Should I have a statement to make on any matter, I will reach out," Figueiredo said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. An experienced keeper at a Dutch zoo has died days after being mauled in a leopard enclosure, the safari park has confirmed.
The woman, who had worked at Beekse Bergen park for 40 years, was caring for two Persian leopards in an indoor facility when she was attacked on Saturday.
She sustained injuries to her head and neck and had emergency surgery, but the park confirmed her death on Tuesday.
An independent investigation will be launched into the incident, it added in a statement.
Announcing her death, Beekse Bergen - in the south of the Netherlands - said the keeper began her career there when she was 17 and had worked there on-and-off for four decades.
"Her passing has deeply affected us all, and our hearts go out to her family, friends, and loved ones. At this moment, our primary focus is on supporting her family and her colleagues," the statement added.
The two leopards, which are usually kept away from staff, had been brought inside due to bad weather conditions.
It is not clear exactly what happened in the enclosure because there are no CCTV cameras inside.
Local news website NL Times reported that despite her injuries she managed to alert colleagues via her walkie-talkie. She was then taken to hospital in a helicopter in a critical condition.
A park spokesperson told Omroep Brabant, a local media outlet, that the leopards were behaving naturally and they would not be euthanised.
"They are, and remain, predators."
Beekse Bergen said it would create a memorial location for guests and staff members to share their condolences.

ce5aa207de50.text: President Trump applauded Quebec's new separatist premier Tuesday, continuing to jab at Ottawa despite fragile trade talks that seemed to be gaining momentum. The big picture: Even as Trump's top economic adviser suggested a deal to ease the ongoing trade war is possible, the president has continue to antagonize Canada. The U.S. recently accused Canada of trying to influence American elections through retaliatory tariffs, which Canadian officials have denied. Meanwhile, Trump's continued to antagonize Canada from the campaign trail, saying at a Mississippi stop Monday that it was "charging us massive tariffs" and has "treated us badly." Driving the news: In a brief shoutout Tuesday, the president congratulated Paul St-Pierre Plamondon for his win some three weeks ago. While a recent vote stymied an Albertan separatist push , St-Pierre Plamondon has vowed to hold Quebec's third referendum on independence, though he's said it wouldn't happen until after Trump leaves office. St-Pierre Plamondon's center-left Parti Québécois won 60 of 127 seats, leaving it four short of a majority. It would likely need support from a fellow separatist party to advance a referendum. Prime Minister Mark Carney has emphasized the importance of Canadian unity as the nation faces unprecedented hostility from the American president. Trump shared an Irish Times article that framed the Quebec vote as a "blow to Mark Carney" that could "hamper" his "efforts to maintain national unity against Trump." Zoom out: Trump on Tuesday also congratulated British Columbia's premier-designate, Lorne Doerkson, after his Conservatives swung the province rightward. "Conservatives are moving strong in Canada!" the president wrote . Doerkson, however, has rejected suggestions that he's aligned with the president, similar to St-Pierre Plamondon. Friction point: The U.S. Embassy in Canada last week accused Canadian leaders of trying to influence American politics with reciprocal tariffs on politically important products and states in the U.S. The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. The intrigue: White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett said in a Fox interview Sunday that negotiations with Canada have "picked up" and are "gathering steam." Carney told reporters Monday trade talks had intensified slightly since the talks last fell apart in August . Midterm politics are complicating Trump's tariff agenda, Axios' Courtenay Brown reports. Last week, the the White House exempted certain Canadian imports from 50% tariffs following pressure from Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) . Collins pledged to seek to seek further tariff relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada. The bottom line: Trump relationship with Canada has been tumultuous — rattled by trade tensions and the president's persistent "51st state" threats. When asked to choose, Florida’s likely voters have picked protecting the environment over economic growth by more than 2 to 1, a margin that surprised even the pollster who asked the question.
In a University of North Florida poll released last week, 61 percent of respondents said state and local officials should prioritize the environment “even at the risk of curbing economic growth.” Twenty-six percent chose growth. Registered Republicans sided with the environment 48 percent to 35 percent, and so did a plurality of 2024 voters who backed Donald Trump.
“I expected probably [the] environment to win narrowly, but this was a blowout,” said Sean Freeder, who directs UNF’s Public Opinion Research Lab.
Less than two weeks before Election Day, that sentiment has echoed through Florida’s U.S. Senate race between Republican Ashley Moody, the incumbent, and Democrat Angie Nixon, a state representative. Instead of a broad climate debate, it shows up in specific fights over data centers, power bills, hurricane recovery and the fixes either candidate can offer.
The race is closer than many expected in a state Trump won by 13 points in 2024. The UNF poll showed Moody, whom Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed in 2025 to serve the rest of Marco Rubio’s term, ahead 49 percent to 45 percent, down 8 points from July. Nixon outraised Moody by nearly $2 million in the third quarter, but Moody and her affiliated committees had about $7.1 million on hand on Oct.1, compared with about $4.5 million for Nixon. The two will not debate.
Nixon’s sharpest environmental position is on data centers. “There needs to be a moratorium,” she told Inside Climate News. “You cannot build any more data centers.” Her campaign platform calls for no new construction “before there are real federal guardrails.”
The Sierra Club, whose political arm has endorsed Nixon, also wants federal rules. “Absent those, yes, we support a statewide moratorium,” said Susannah Randolph, director of Sierra Club Florida.
In June, Walton County commissioners voted unanimously to prohibit large data centers. In Polk County, residents are fighting a proposed $2.6 billion project on a former phosphate mine in Fort Meade, where Nixon held a town hall last month.
Moody, whose campaign did not respond to requests for comment, has said data center decisions belong to communities and states. “It needs to be up to the people of a community or a state to decide what works best for them,” she said in a Fox News interview last month. In September, she cosponsored the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would push utility regulators to make large data centers cover the grid costs of serving them.
“If billion-dollar tech companies want to build a massive data center, Floridians should not be left to foot the bill,” she said at the time.
The Ratepayer Protection Act, which passed the House 417-3 but has not cleared the Senate, would direct state utility regulators to consider standards requiring large data centers that draw more than 100 megawatts—roughly the electricity used by 65,000 Florida homes—to pay the full cost of new power plants, transmission lines and grid upgrades built to serve them. It would also have regulators consider requiring those customers to post financial guarantees before construction begins and to cover costs if they walk away from a contract early.
Florida’s new data center law, Senate Bill 484, signed in May, goes further. It already requires utilities to make large data center customers pay their full cost of service so those expenses don’t shift to other ratepayers, and it applies to more facilities than the federal bill.
“Anybody that would be covered by the Ratepayer Protection Act is already covered by Senate Bill 484,” said Ted Kury, director of energy studies at the University of Florida’s Public Utility Research Center. “When it comes to electricity, essentially all they’re saying is, ‘Hey, the state PSC has to do their job.’”
A national moratorium, he added, would likely be challenged by states that want data centers, “and the federal government would probably lose.” (The research center’s sponsors include Florida Power & Light and the Florida Public Service Commission.)

Randolph was blunter about Moody’s sponsorship weeks before the election: “The timing is really suspicious and doesn’t smell good.”
Both candidates also pitch themselves as capable of offering relief from rising power bills. Nixon said she would “call for investigations” when rate increases follow large utility campaign contributions. Moody has built her affordability message around the federal tax cuts she voted for.
Florida Power & Light customers are absorbing the biggest rate hike in the utility’s history, approved last November: $945 million in 2026 and $705 million in 2027, with more on the horizon. Retail rates are set by the Florida PSC, not Congress. “As far as electricity prices at the state level, there’s not a lot that a U.S. senator could do,” Kury said.
What a senator can affect is federal tax policy. Moody voted for Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which ended a 30 percent tax credit for homeowners who install rooftop solar and set earlier deadlines for utility-scale solar and wind projects to qualify for federal credits. Kury said the law’s effect on bills varies by utility, because taxpayers fund the credits, too. “The people always pay,” he said. “All the policymakers decide is how and when.”
Disaster recovery is the other pressure point in the race. Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin as a Category 2 storm on Oct. 9, and Moody is leading a congressional push for a major disaster declaration. An inquiry into the deaths of 33 detainees in Nigeria's Minna state has found they died as a result of severe overcrowding, poor ventilation and failure by officers to respond to distress calls.
Forensic and medical evidence showed the "entirely preventable" deaths had resulted from acute respiratory failure linked to prolonged confinement, aggravated by heat stress and dehydration.
The evidence did not support initial claims of a disease outbreak.
The detainees were found dead on 17 September while being held by the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps on suspicion of illegal mining. The investigation found that the mining sites had been licensed.
Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo said those found responsible for the deaths would face the full force of the law.
He added that the detention hall had been cleaned before investigators arrived, raising concerns about possible attempts to compromise evidence.
Implicated officers will face suspension and the report would be forwarded to the attorney general of the federation for further legal action, Tunji-Ojo said.
The investigating committee found that the raid on the miners had been conducted without an approved operational order, proper planning or consultation with the Mining Marshals Unit.
It said that 50 detainees had been held in a cell measuring about 20 sq m, with no running water or functioning toilet, and inadequate food, drinking water and airflow.
Adults and minors were detained together, and some detainees were held beyond lawful detention periods.
Officers reportedly ignored repeated calls for help, despite a medical worker having raised concerns about the conditions.
"Detainees repeatedly banged on cell doors and walls, shouted for assistance and pleaded for water," said the head of the investigating team, Jonathan Kure.
"These distress calls were heard by officers assigned to nearby duties... but were not acted upon."
Kure said the detention conditions amounted to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment.
"The tragedy demonstrates the consequences of systemic disregard for detention standards, supervisory responsibilities and the welfare of persons in custody," he added.
The investigating committee also recommended compensation of 30m naira (Â£16,683; $22,285) for each of the bereaved families and 10m naira for each survivor.

Twin brothers from Ghana and an American woman have pleaded guilty to being part of an international criminal network that defrauded people on dating sites and social media.
The group targeted elderly people in the US and Europe, using fake identities to lure their victims into believing they were in a romantic relationship, before persuading them to transfer large sums of money into bank accounts in Ghana.
The 22-year-old twins, Jamal and Kamal Abubakari, and 53-year-old Amanda Joy Opoku-Boachie from Hawaii face up to 20 years in jail and will be sentenced next year.
Between July 2024 - April 2026, the victims collectively lost $9m (Â£6.7m).
While many of them were from Ohio - where the charges were brought - other victims were located in 24 other US states, as well as Germany and Austria.
As part of the plea, the Abubakaris and Opoku-Boachie agreed to forfeit pieces of jewellery which investigators seized during their arrest, including luxury watches, rings, chains and earrings.
The three accused go by several names:
- Jamal Abubakari, also known as Jamal Abubakar and Arrangement
- Kamal Abubakari, also known as Kamal Abubakar and Lancaster
- Joy Opoku-Boachie, also known as Amanda Joy Glum and Amanda Joy Kessei Bierman
In recent months, US authorities have stepped up their crackdown on criminal networks operating in the US and West Africa which seek to defraud elderly Americans.
Earlier this month, FBI Director Kash Patel said it had made hundreds of arrests after dismantling a scam centre in Ghana.
In June, a Ghanaian social media influencer known as Abu Trica, whose real name is Frederick Kumi, was extradited to the US to face trial for allegedly running a romance scam that defrauded elderly Americans of more than $8m (Â£5.9m).
He targeted victims through social media and online dating platforms, and is accused of requesting money or valuables under false pretences such as urgent medical needs.
The case against Kumi is being prosecuted under the US Elder Abuse Prevention and Prosecution law. He denies all the charges against him.

A controversial Islamic cleric in Nigeria has been murdered outside his home in the northern state of Katsina.
Two assailants arrived on a motorcycle and shot Yahaya Masussuka in the town of Dutsin-Ma as he was saying goodbye to visitors on Monday evening, sources told the BBC.
The 47-year-old preacher and one of his guests, who was also shot, were rushed to hospital but both were pronounced dead by the attending doctor, police said.
It is not clear why Masussuka was targeted, but the cleric had received death threats on social media where he posted videos in which he rejected some elements of mainstream Islam, including what happens to people after their death.
It is widely believed in Islam that a person's soul will be questioned in the grave by two angels. If they answer correctly, their soul sleeps peacefully until the day of judgement - if not it will be tormented.
This understanding comes from what is known as the Hadith, a collection of texts believed to be the spoken words and actions of the Prophet Muhammad.
This serves as a key source of Islamic knowledge to help interpret the Quran, the central religious text of Islam.
But Masussuka based his teachings mainly on what was in Islam's holy book, questioned some of the hadiths - and did not believe that the dead were reawakened and questioned.
He was once jailed for nine months because he teased some respected scholars over their belief in this hadith and other teachings.
Masussuka, who had two wives and seven children, began preaching at the age of 13 in Quranic schools.
He later attended Al-Azhar University in Egypt and later went to Oman for further studies.
At his home, he had a studio where he would record videos of his teachings for broadcast on social media for his followers.
The cleric was also outspoken about violent extremism, radicalisation and openly advocated for interfaith dialogue and peaceful coexistence between Muslims and Christians, who make up nearly equal parts of Nigeria's population.
Thousands of Christians and Muslims have been killed in ethnic and religious violence here over the past 25 years.
For Masussuka's efforts, Nigeria's Network for Good Governance and Transparency honoured him with a Peace Ambassador Award last year.
Six other prominent Muslim preachers have been murdered over the last two decades in northern Nigeria - several targeted by Boko Haram for criticising the jihadist group that began its insurgency in 2009.
Founded in north-eastern Nigeria, it opposes Western culture, education, the secular government - and its political goal is the creation of an Islamic state.
Additional reporting by BBC Pidgin

A bank of white freezers hums away at a former watch factory in central London. Inside: dozens of small boxes with barcoded glass tubes, collectively containing one hundred billion genes. Just two boxes may hold 10 times more information than all the text on the internet, says Dr Oliver Vince, the facility's co-founder.
His firm, Basecamp Research, plans to collect as much DNA as possible to create an artificial intelligence that can speak the language of biology, in the same way that US and Chinese tech firms have hoovered up written material online to create Large Language Models (LLMs), the basis of current AI systems.
Vince, like many in business and academic research, believes AI will supercharge scientific research. But increasingly, it also comes with controversy.
Last month, OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, said it had solved one of maths' great unsolved problems, relating to the famous NavierâStokes equations. The company said its AI agents had cracked it in 88 hours. The body that runs a prize for whoever can solve the problem said it had "apparently been settled", but that its review would take time.
But hours before the announcement, Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University, went public with concerns. He formed an independent team with Levent AlpÃ¶ge, a mathematician employed by day by the rival company Anthropic.
They had been working towards the same goal, and kept their drafts in OpenAI's coding tool, Codex. Buckmaster said that his co-researcher was tipped off that news of their progress had "reached" OpenAI, though he did not specify how. He asked whether his research, stored in Codex, could have fed into OpenAI's own work, though he stressed he was "not accusing anyone of anything".
OpenAI said that nobody at the company, human or AI, saw the other teams' work before it was published. Initially it said that while unlikely, it could not "rule out" that anonymised data from use of its products may have helped improve its models. Days later, it said Buckmaster's Codex prompts from the two months before the announcement "could not have influenced the system in any way".
It's a complicated story; we still don't fully know what happened. But it highlights a growing issue about the use of AI in science. Usually, those words make us conjure up images of robots building terrible genetically-engineered viruses, or chemical weapons, to wipe out humanity. But there's a more subtle problem that hasn't attracted the same headline-grabbing attention: that AI could undermine faith in the scientific process, raising questions about the novelty and accuracy of research.
And there's another concern. It's well known that AI chatbots like Claude or Gemini can sometimes hallucinate things that simply aren't true. They will tell you about a film that never existed, or a quote that was never said. Now there is evidence that this is increasingly happening in science. Eventually, it's feared, it will become difficult to separate true scientific discovery from AI-generated fiction.
And all of this could threaten to erode - if not explode - the rock on which scientific research rests: trust.
A 'watershed moment'
One threat is to scientific journals, the guardians of scientific integrity, which are seen to be failing to deal with a tsunami of AI-generated distortions.
"Generative AI has basically disrupted the whole scientific process," says Dalmeet Singh Chawla, a science journalist who has spent a decade reporting on research misconduct.
He tells the BBC that publishers' integrity staff - the people who screen submissions for accuracy and reliability - will need to "drastically increase [in number and effort] if they're anywhere near the fight". He says: "Right now, it seems like they're not."
On the face of it, AI seems just the right tool to power scientific research. Scientists deal with huge amounts of information. Telescopes and particle accelerators, for example, collect billions of data points â too large for the brain to comprehend. AI can pick the scientific highlights from the surrounding humdrum.
The poster child of scientific AI is the UK-based firm Google DeepMind, which in 2020 solved one of biology's biggest problems: how proteins in living things fold into their precise shapes.
It may sound dull, but proteins are the tiny machines that make life work, and the shapes they fold into determine what they can do; from building cells and fighting infection to helping form the tissues and organs of the body.
Before AI, scientists had to conduct time-consuming experiments in the lab. Then, Google DeepMind developed an AI model called AlphaFold that accurately predicted 200 million protein folds in just one year.
The equivalent experimental work would have taken hundreds of millions of years in laboratories. The firm gave the results away for free to researchers. The head of DeepMind and the project's lead scientist were both awarded the Nobel Prize for Chemistry.
It was big hugs all round.
Dr Pushmeet Kohli, who leads DeepMind's science work, told me that AlphaFold could be seen as a "watershed moment".
Questions over AI's work
But elsewhere, the use of AI in science has come with accusations of hype. Some computer models are accused of exaggerating the significance of their findings, with the human researchers that oversee them then believing some of the claims without enough scepticism.
Basking in its success over AlphaFold, for example, DeepMind turned its attention to predicting the structure of new materials. The work could lead to the development of better batteries, cheaper solar cells and electronic components that are not dependent on rare earth elements. (In theory, no-one would need to argue about mining rights ever again, and Greenland would be safe from invasion.)
A DeepMind model came up with what the firm claimed were more than two million new crystal structures, announced as "nearly 800 years worth of knowledge" released in one go. Of those, some 380,000 w

23730410d376.text: Senate Republicans see Iowa moving their way and Ohio slipping, with pessimism growing over Alaska and Kansas. Why it matters: Even when they squint, top Republicans struggle to see a majority beyond 51 seats, according to half a dozen senior operatives. ✈️ A combination of paid media and Air Force One visits has bolstered GOP confidence that they'll hold South Carolina and Mississippi . But across the map, the outlook looks bleak, with only a few bright spots. Zoom out: Republicans are fighting a two-front war: unprecedented Democratic enthusiasm and undeniable Republican apathy. 🏈 President Trump's strategy is to whip up the MAGA faithful with rallies in the reddest parts of red states. 😱 "The Red Scream is my biggest concern , not the blue wave," said Alex Castellanos, a veteran Republican consultant who has worked to help Trump get elected. ‼️ "Republicans and independents are going to be screaming for attention, and many of them, including those who voted for Trump, may show their frustration by not showing up." Zoom in: Texas is starting to look like a late-season football showdown against an SEC rival: The GOP is still in the game, but defeat seems like a real possibility. 🌾 In Kansas, Sen. Roger Marshall (R) has stopped the bleeding, but it's unclear whether there's enough time left to save his seat. 🛥️ Republicans are quietly bullish on Michigan, but they recognize that the demographics have to break heavily in their favor, especially among Black voters. By the numbers: The math hasn't changed, but Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) sees multiple paths to 51 seats. No one disputes that North Carolina is going to have a Democratic senator. It seems like another lifetime ago that Republicans were talking seriously about flipping Georgia. If just two of the next tier of Ohio, Kansas and Alaska flip, the Senate would be split 50-50 before factoring in other competitive races, like Michigan, Iowa and Maine. 🦞 In Maine, Republicans and Democrats are consumed by competing fears. Republicans are terrified that a national wave will be big enough to wash away Sen. Susan Collins. Democrats, burned by her unforeseen survival six years ago, refuse to trust even the polls showing them ahead. 🎣 Between the lines: Maine and Alaska may be separated by more than 3,000 miles, but they pose a similar challenge for pollsters: small, overfished electorates where voters are increasingly unwilling to pick up the phone and bite on yet another survey. Both could also see delays in their final results — potentially keeping the majority in limbo for days or weeks, as we told you last night.

A decade after world leaders signed the legally binding Paris Agreement to combat climate change, the crisis’ health harms are getting worse and progress is lagging, according to a new report from leading international scientists.
The 10th annual Lancet Countdown report, published Tuesday, is authored by 146 researchers from more than 30 countries, led by University College London and produced in collaboration with the World Health Organization. Following a slew of record-breaking findings in last year’s report, the authors found that heat, famine, disaster and disease are costing millions of lives around the world. Health harms from climate change, they say, have accelerated faster in the decade since the Paris Agreement than they did in the decade prior.
These harms are global, but they fall disproportionately on lower-income nations that have contributed relatively little to the climate crisis.
Meanwhile, rising energy demand, continued fossil fuel reliance and a slow transition to clean energy mean the world is failing to respond to the speed and scale of the hazards.
“Climate change is not only getting worse, but it’s getting worse a lot faster than it used to, and that has to do with the fact that year on year we’re reaching record levels of greenhouse gas emissions,” said Marina Romanello, executive director of the Lancet Countdown. “It’s a stark call to action.”
Recent months saw catastrophic floods, wildfires and heat waves, and news that the world is on course to overshoot the key 1.5 degree Celsius warming threshold set in the Paris Agreement within the next few years.
The report’s authors called on the World Health Organization and member states to declare climate change a global health emergency, and for health to be centered in global talks to reduce emissions and transition away from fossil fuels. The next major opportunity is in November at the 31st United Nations Conference of the Parties on climate, known as COP31.
“The evidence is undeniable: climate change is one of the greatest threats to health facing humanity,” said Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director-general of the World Health Organization, in a statement with the report.
The report’s authors emphasized that global investments in clean energy have brought some relief: From 2016 to 2023, cleaner air avoided an estimated 323,000 annual deaths in a little more than half of countries surveyed, with leading gains in China and the U.S. But globally, that was balanced out by increased deaths in the other 46 percent of countries.
The average number of people dying each year from extreme heat has grown in the last decade. In 2023—the most recent year with complete data—heat was linked to a record 710,000 estimated deaths. That’s more than the lives lost to HIV or malaria in the same year. And more than 70 percent of those deaths are attributable to human-caused climate change, according to the report.
Between 2016 and 2023, climate change is estimated to have caused almost 3 million heat deaths, the authors found.
Heat also has serious impacts on people’s livelihoods, and carved an estimated $1.07 trillion of potential income out of the global economy as high temperatures kept people from work, the report concluded. Southeast Asia and Africa were hit hardest, as were the agriculture and construction sectors.

ac7df6c28a05.text: Senate leaders could be guessing who will control the chamber well into November, thanks to a slew of tight races and state-specific voting rules. Why it matters: A GOP majority would ease the pressure on Senate Majority Leader John Thune to move quickly on nominations, while a Democratic majority would give Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer more leverage in the lame-duck session. If the chamber splits 50/50, leaders will have to start negotiating their power-sharing agreement. Zoom in: Four states could leave the majority in limbo. Alaska: Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) is trying to fend off former Rep. Mary Peltola (D). Alaska election results have taken weeks to finalize because of the vast state's transportation challenges, mail ballots and ranked-choice tabulation. The Trump Justice Department is preemptively trying to block results from being finalized if Sullivan narrowly loses. Maine's ranked-choice voting could lengthen the vote tallying if neither Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) nor Democratic nominee Troy Jackson gets more than 50% in the first round. Kansas' three-day grace period for mail-in ballots could delay results in the race between Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton and Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.). It is far closer than expected. In Texas, a dragged-out recount could be coming. A candidate can request one if the margin is less than 10% of the winner's vote total — which is likely to happen between state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) and state Rep. James Talarico (D). The candidate who requests it has to pay. The clock: Congress currently plans to leave for the holidays on Dec. 18. But if Republicans lose both the House and Senate , Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) wants senators to stay in town through the holidays (yes, Thanksgiving and Christmas) to work on a massive GOP reconciliation package they can pass without Democratic support. The big picture: Congress has a long to-do list either way, including funding the government past Dec. 11, passing emergency defense spending and potentially raising the debt ceiling. It needs to pass the National Defense Authorization Act, Farm Bill and permitting reform, reauthorize the warrantless wiretap authority under FISA Section 702 and confirm nominations before they expire at the end of the year. The bottom line: "I'm guessing that's a possibility this year," Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.) told reporters today about working in D.C. through the holiday recess.

fc3ee73e15dd.text: Israelis turned out in record numbers for their first election since the Oct. 7 attacks and the war in Gaza. Projections show opposition parties won more seats than the coalition led by Prime Minister Netanyahu, potentially setting the stage for a change in government. But Netanyahu’s opponents do not have enough seats to form a majority, leading to weeks of negotiations. Nick Schifrin reports. Geoff Bennett: Israelis turned out in record numbers for their first election since the October 7 terrorist attacks that launched the war in Gaza. Amna Nawaz: And, according to projections, opposition parties have won more seats in Parliament than the coalition led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, potentially setting the stage for a change in government. Nick Schifrin is live for us in Tel Aviv tonight -- Nick. Nick Schifrin: Amna, this is the headquarters for Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition coalition. His party and his supporters are emphasizing that they, along with the Arab parties, won many more seats than Netanyahu's coalition. And Netanyahu's coalition lost many seats. But, Amna, the bottom line is that this coalition does not appear to have a path toward forming a majority government after what many Israelis call one of the country's most consequential elections. Tonight in Tel Aviv, the party that wants to unseat Israel's longest-serving prime minister says they have a mandate to change the country. But 40 miles up the road in Jerusalem, Netanyahu's party is saying it won the most votes and there's no path to an opposition government. There are 120 seats in the Israeli Parliament, which means a coalition needs 61 to form a majority government. Netanyahu's coalition is estimated to have won 50 seats. Eisenkot's coalition is estimated to have won more, 53, but not enough to secure a majority. Arab parties, who are anti-Netanyahu, have an estimated record 17, but it's unlikely that Eisenkot's coalition allies will agree to work with them. We have been traveling through the country in the lead-up to the election, and there is a widespread perception that this moment is historically fractious and the election existential. Jonathan Barsade: Doesn't matter what side of the political spectrum you're on. Israel is at a crossroads. Nick Schifrin: Jonathan Barsade is a dual American-Israeli citizen and the president of the nonpartisan America-Israel Democracy Coalition. Jonathan Barsade: These elections are going to determine what direction Israel is going to go and how Israel is going to look for the next 40, 50 years. That's a sentiment everyone -- they feel it. Nick Schifrin: He's helped lead the largest ever effort to bring Israeli expats back to the country to vote since Israel has no mail-in voting. Some 70,000 have returned. Including Ruth Mekel, who's wise enough not to give her age. She flew here from New York to vote against Netanyahu. Ruthie Mekel, Israeli Voter: These are really critical, critical elections, historic elections, in order to prevent this government from ending the democracy and starting an orthodox religious way of life. Nick Schifrin: A few miles to the south, voting's a family affair for 3-year-old Michael... Avshalom Seri, Rishon LeZion, Israel, Resident: He's a good citizen. Nick Schifrin: ... who helped his grandfather also vote against Netanyahu; 75-year-old Avshalom Seri says new leadership could bring peace. Avshalom Seri: I hope that we will come with different leaders, leaders that -- thinking for peace. We have children. We have grandchildren, and we think about them, the new generation. We fight so much. That's enough. The time for peace. Nick Schifrin: But Netanyahu and his supporters believe Israel's peace comes from his strength. Woman: This is the work of a genius. Nick Schifrin: And like a chess player, they argue only he has the strategy to take on Israel's enemies, and only he has the relationship with President Trump to finish the job in Iran. Maor Vaknin, Likud Adviser (through interpreter): With the help of God, in the next four years, Bibi will continue to do more things with Trump in the two years that Trump has left. We will solve this problem, which is called Hamas, Hezbollah, Lebanon, Syria, Iran, and then we succeed in cutting off the head of the snake, as Bibi promised. Nick Schifrin: Forty-four-old Shimi Elias also brought his son Omri to vote. He usually votes for Netanyahu, but this year voted for Netanyahu ally, right-wing Minister of Finance Bezalel Smotrich. Shimi Elias, Israeli Voter: The government since the war, I'm happy with what they achieved. Nick Schifrin: Tonight, those divides remain, and a country hoping for a decisive decision once again faces uncertainty. Amna Nawaz: And Nick is back with us now from Tel Aviv. So, Nick, without either side winning a majority here, what happens now, and specifically what does that mean for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu? Nick Schifrin: So, as you know, Amna, there will be a lot of horse-trading over the next few days and the next few weeks and perhaps even the next few months. Perhaps the most likely outcome from the Eisenkot campaign, or at least the best outcome from them, would be what's known as a minority government. They would form a government with fewer than 61 seats. But, as we laid out in the piece, that would require collaborating with the Arab parties. And inside of Eisenkot's coalition, that's already been rejected. Now, of course, in Israeli politics, a lot of things can be said before the election, and that changes after the election, but right now there's not a lot of popularity or support for the idea of getting Arab support to create that government. Now, President Trump and his aides would like to see some kind of unity government, Netanyahu and Eisenkot working together. Eisenkot and every single one of the leading opposition party, the leading -- the leaders of the opposition parties, have absolutely refused that scenario. So if there is no minority gove

85f1976054cd.text: White evangelical Christians have been among President Trump’s most loyal supporters for more than a decade, and our new PBS News/NPR/Marist poll shows that most still approve of him. But signs of slippage are emerging ahead of the midterms. Stephanie Sy reports on the overlap of politics and faith. Geoff Bennett: White evangelical Christians have been among President Trump's most loyal supporters for more than a decade now. And while our new PBS News/NPR/Marist poll shows that most still approve of the president, there are signs that support may be slipping as the midterms approach. Here's Stephanie Sy. Stephanie Sy: On a Wednesday night at Village Church in Blythewood, South Carolina, Pastor Erik Estep is preaching from his pre-midterm election sermon, the Bible and politics. Pastor Erik Estep, Village Church: I believe the church is the bulwark of truth for our nation. And it will take people like you and churches like this church to protect this nation spiritually and morally. Stephanie Sy: White evangelical Christians have been the bedrock of Donald Trump's support for more than a decade, and they largely still are. In the latest PBS News/NPR/Marist poll, 66 percent say they approve of the job Trump is doing as president, 26 points higher than the number of Americans overall who say the same. As Trump rallies his base ahead of the midterm elections, nearly three-quarters of white evangelicals also plan to back Republicans for Congress. For Trump, it's a bond that once seemed unlikely. In 2016, candidate Trump rocketed to the top of the Republican primary, a thrice-married New York real estate mogul caught on tape bragging about groping women and accused of relationships with more than one porn star. President Donald Trump: I stand before you today to fulfill one of my highest and most important duties under the United States Constitution, the nomination of a Supreme Court justice. Stephanie Sy: But, as president, he accomplished what has long driven many Christians at the polls, his appointment of three conservative Supreme Court justices, which led to the historic overturning of Roe v. Wade and a rollback of abortion protections for millions of American women. Estep acknowledges his congregants don't all vote alike, but making abortion illegal is one issue where they are mostly aligned. Pastor Erik Estep: To vote according to what our faith prescribes us to vote. Some people have different perspectives, but there's not much of a different perspective when it comes to issues of abortion and life. I think the Bible's pretty clear. Stephanie Sy: But even among evangelicals, Trump's support has slipped, reflecting an overall fraying of his coalition. His approval rating among those that voted for him has dropped 12 points since the start of his second term. That falloff is particularly steep among Latinos and young voters in other recent polling. Even at Village Church in South Carolina, some are wavering. Cynthia Carroll, South Carolina Voter: I was a Republican. I voted Donald Trump into -- as president. And now I'm more on the fence between conservative and a Democrat. Stephanie Sy: Until recently, that loyalty had survived some striking moments, like when conservative Charlie Kirk was assassinated last year and his widow, Erika, chose to forgive his killer. Erika Kirk, CEO, Turning Point USA: I forgive him because it was what Christ did and is what Charlie would do. Stephanie Sy: President Trump took a different stance. President Donald Trump: That's where I disagreed with Charlie. I hate my opponent. Stephanie Sy: And this spring, the president posted an AI image of himself appearing as a Christ-like healer. President Donald Trump: I did post it. Stephanie Sy: After Christian leaders labeled it blasphemous, Trump deleted it, explaining he thought the image portrayed him as a doctor, which he also is not. Robert Jones, CEO, Public Religion Research Institute: I think part of it is really about a vision of the country that he has promised them. Stephanie Sy: Robert Jones, president of the Public Religion Research Institute, says the evangelical support Trump does still enjoy is rooted in a certain vision of America. Robert Jones: The message is, we're a white Christian country. We're losing that identity. But if you stick with me, I'm going to make sure that we keep that identity. Stephanie Sy: But voters who identify as Christian may have more options this election. Christian faith leaders are running for the Senate as Democrats in Kansas and Texas. In reliably red South Carolina, where the Senate race is unusually tight. Republicans are trying to energize evangelical support for Darline Graham by focusing on transgender issues. President Donald Trump: The Democrat who Darline is running to defeat is a far left political hack who supports transgender for everybody and believes in telling confused children they're trapped in the wrong body. Stephanie Sy: During a recent campaign rally in the state, Trump painted Democrats as enemies of conservative values. Robert Jones: So when you have, like, that willingness to like literally demonize your political opponents, and then you have got a group that has been attached to you by party and religion, it sets up a kind of toxic environment. Stephanie Sy: For his part, Pastor Erik Estep does not endorse specific candidates or a party in his sermon. Pastor Erik Estep: We think that it falls on pastors. If you want people to respond and to get out and to be to be heard, well, there has to be some sort of motivation. Stephanie Sy: What motivates his congregants this year may well be critical on Election Day. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Stephanie Sy.

887a84ce72f8.text: Indonesia is battling its worst wildfires in more than a decade, made worse by El Niño. Many were deliberately set to clear land for farming, including palm oil plantations. More than 12,000 schools across Indonesia have closed because of the toxic haze. Nathaniel Undas, a school principal and photographer, has been documenting the fires on social media. Amna Nawaz: Indonesia is battling its worst wildfires in more than a decade, made worse by El Nino weather patterns. Many of these fires were deliberately set to clear land for farming, including palm oil plantations. Rain this week brought some relief, but the rainy season isn't expected until next month. More than 12,000 schools across Indonesia have closed because of the toxic haze, which has also spread to neighboring countries. In Central Kalimantan, where children have been out of class for weeks, one school principal and photographer has been documenting the fires on social media. He spoke to us from an empty classroom at the Golden Christian Middle School. Natanael Undas, Photographer: My name is Natanael Undas. I'm a school principal Palangkaraya, Central Kalimantan. It is a kind of rain forest and then a lot of native trees. We got a lot of fruits. We got a lot of tree for timber. But now the sky, it turns yellow. It turns like hell. The last time I saw the blue sky was in August '20. The haze come to our city. And then the fire goes closer, closer, closer and closer. And then, like the last week, it was a really huge fire in the city. I'm really sad, because my student lost a lot of school hour and learning experience. If you go outside in a school hour, probably at 8:00, 9:00 a.m. in the morning, they go outside, they play with other friends without a mask and thinking it's just like a school holiday in the middle of yellow sky. This fire is not natural disaster at all. It is manmade disaster. We're hoping the rain will come soon. Last night, there was a huge rain, even only for 17 to 25 minutes. We're longing to inhale the smell of rain, the smell of air, the smell of wet leaves, the smell of wet land. Last night, when it was raining, I open a little bit of my door, and I try to smell the rain. It's like a smelling the perfume that's mixed with smoke. It's still poisoned, so I need to close it. Not many people knows about what really happening right now, what we are experiencing, especially what we are inhaling. A lot of children are suffering because of respiratory issue. I don't want my daughter having the same experience. I don't want to lose this generation. We still can save this.

5060f9921bf8.text: This year, the 26th president's legacy received a remarkable new tribute: the opening of the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in the Badlands of North Dakota, a landscape that helped shape his lifelong commitment to conservation. Senior arts correspondent Jeffrey Brown recently paid a visit for our arts and culture series, CANVAS. Geoff Bennett: Finally tonight, a birthday salute to Theodore Roosevelt. The nation's 26th president one of its most consequential was born on this day back in 1858. And, this year, his legacy received a remarkable new tribute, the opening of the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in the Badlands of North Dakota, a landscape that helped shape his lifelong commitment to conservation. Our senior arts correspondent, Jeffrey Brown, paid a visit for our arts and culture series, Canvas. Jeffrey Brown: It's a spectacular setting nestled in the rugged Badlands of Western North Dakota, a breathtaking tribute to the life and legacy of Theodore Roosevelt. It's a landscape that deeply impacted T.R., who once said he'd never have become president if not for his time here. And it continues to inspire and move people today. Craig Dykers: We wanted it to feel that it belonged, so that it didn't feel that it just dropped out of the sky. Jeffrey Brown: Yes. Craig Dykers: At the same time, we wanted it to feel fresh and new and different from anything anybody had seen before. Jeffrey Brown: Craig Dykers, co-founder of the international architecture firm Snohetta, helped design the new 93,000-square-foot Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library. Craig Dykers: There's a sensation of what the landscape means that you learn when you move through it. Jeffrey Brown: After settling on this remote location, Dykers camped alone for 12 days in the Badlands searching for inspiration. Craig Dykers: In the wilderness here, the more you go into it, the more you're able to experience what he called lonesome freedom, or lonely freedom. And that's an interesting idea, that you're alone, but you feel free. Normally, we think of being alone as a scary thing, especially in a place that's wild. Jeffrey Brown: Beautiful, but potentially very scary out there, right, if you're alone. Craig Dykers: Yes, if you're alone, but, at a certain point, you and the context around you become one. Jeffrey Brown: The son of wealthy and prominent New Yorkers, Teddy Roosevelt first came to the small town of Medora to hunt bison in 1883. He returned the following year as a heartbroken 25-year-old after writing in his diary: "The light has gone out of my life." Edward O'Keefe: The Women Who Created a President": Theodore Roosevelt came to North Dakota at a time of incredible stress and distress in his life. He had lost his wife and his mother on the same day of different causes in the same house. He healed and he recovered in the Badlands of North Dakota. Jeffrey Brown: Edward O'Keefe is the CEO of the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library Foundation, a nonprofit that raised more than $500 million to complete the project. O'Keefe, author of a biography of T.R. and who now leads public broadcasting's WNET Group in New York City, says Roosevelt's time in North Dakota would shape the rest of his life. Edward O'Keefe: He found resilience in nature. He mourned, and he was depressed when he was in Dakota. And he finally got to live that life that he'd only read about in books. Theodore Roosevelt felt that North Dakota saved his life. Jeffrey Brown: So far, large crowds have poured in since the library opened July 4, offering visitors a chance to learn about a president who left an indelible, if complicated, impression on American life. A champion of conservation and protector of public lands, Roosevelt was also a champion of military might and expansion abroad. Edward O'Keefe: Theodore Roosevelt is like a Rorschach test. What you see in him says more about you than it does about him. Republicans, Democrats, independents, everyone loves T.R., right? That's the beauty of Theodore Roosevelt. He brings people together. Jeffrey Brown: And while it's a presidential library in name only, Roosevelt's personal papers are mostly scattered elsewhere, some of his most famous speeches light up the walls, and visitors can see photos and artifacts from every part of his life, from his student days at Harvard, to a hat and single-action Colt revolver from his time as a New York City police commissioner. Edward O'Keefe: Theodore Roosevelt later said, it's better to wear out than to rust out. And he did it every day of his life. He lived only to 60 years old, and those were very, very packed 60 years. Jeffrey Brown: Other highlights include his custom-tailored Rough Rider uniform worn during the Spanish-American war. AI ACTOR: I wanted every guest to feel the worth of their talents. Jeffrey Brown: And there's even an AI hologram of Roosevelt designed by Microsoft that takes questions. Mr. President, what do you hope people visiting your library take away from it? AI ACTOR: I hope visitors leave knowing a single thing. We have power to protect wild places just as I did. Edward O'Keefe: Theodore Roosevelt wrote a letter in 1918, a year before he died. He said: "If I could keep one memory of my entire life, it would be my experiences as a rancher and a cowboy in Dakota." Jeffrey Brown: Using heavy timber, rammed earth walls, and Many materials native to the region, Dyker says the library was designed to give visitors a chance to reflect, all while taking in the surrounding natural beauty, from a walkable roof above, to rocking chairs below. Craig Dykers: If you look at the shape, it has a shape that's characteristic of the low-lying Badlands in the distance. It's not the same, but it has the feeling of something you might find out here. Narrator: Here we have a group of beings who are not able to protect themselves. What we know about Ukraine-Russia truce in Oleshky, brokered by Melania Trump

4f7b97b509b5.text: Some Democrats are making a play for segments of the "Make America Healthy Again" base, hoping pitches about food safety and environmental health will attract voters disillusioned with the Trump administration's lack of progress on those fronts. Why it matters: Policies around cleaning up the food supply and agricultural practices helped forge a coalition that's credited with helping President Trump win a second term. But disagreements over issues like pesticide use are fueling speculation that MAHA voters may not show up in force to help Republicans in the midterm elections — and may be persuaded to put their faith in Democrats instead. Driving the news: Some Democrats say they're the party better positioned to take on established interests through regulation and are honing messaging with an eye toward the 2028 presidential race. The Center for American Progress, an influential progressive think tank, recently released a proposal focused on healthier foods and reducing harmful chemicals alongside polling showing Democrats are poised to claim the agenda as their own. "I do think the MAHA grassroots movement has raised the salience of some issues where Democrats have an opportunity to align, particularly on chemicals and pesticides," said Topher Spiro, an author of the CAP report. "I think that these are issues that have been percolating for a long time, and that, frankly, Democrats haven't done a great job of prioritizing." "If you're looking at who are the swing voters in this electoral environment, they overlap very highly with voters who care about these issues," added Becca Siegel, chief insights officer at CAP. Though affordability concerns have dominated the midterm elections, some Democratic lawmakers and candidates have already backed legislation or policy agendas that overlap with MAHA themes. Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed last month released a proposal titled "Building a Healthier America" that included calls for banning certain pesticides — a key unrealized MAHA goal — and healthier school meals. House Democrats' health care working group included a section in its policy agenda called "Reclaiming MAHA and Protecting American Families." Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) — a potential 2028 presidential candidate — has publicly supported some food policies advanced by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and pushed legislation increasing the liability of companies for potential harm from pesticides. By the numbers: CAP's polling found that 37% of Trump voters are open to voting for a Democratic candidate running on a platform that addresses core MAHA issues, and that Democrats are more trusted than Republicans on health, food and environmental issues. Nonpartisan polling from the Annenberg Public Policy Center found that much higher percentages of the public support MAHA-aligned policies than identify as MAHA supporters. 80% of respondents said they support labeling ultra-processed foods, 79% support removing ultra-processed foods from school lunches and 76% support removing artificial dyes from food. That's even though only a quarter said they are MAHA supporters. Yes, but: One prominent MAHA faction is built around medical freedom and questioning the safety of certain vaccines — a nonstarter for many Democrats who've been sharply critical of Kennedy's health policies. But the Annenberg polling found that MAHA vaccine priorities are much less popular than its food agenda, and that even among the faithful, some vaccine agenda items barely have majority support. State of play: The latest blow to the MAHA coalition came last week, when Trump health adviser and MAHA advocate Calley Means resigned from his post, reportedly over the slow pace of food-related policy changes. Means insisted on X that there's been unprecedented policy and cultural change since the start of the second Trump administration and that the "movement is just getting started." But other MAHA leaders have publicly shared their frustration. "To be clear, [Kennedy] is a hero but his commitments to our movement are being stalled by corporate capture and special interests at the very top of the White House," Vani Hari, an influencer also known as Food Babe, posted on X . "The progress he is trying to make is getting killed by the corporations poisoning us," she added. What they're saying: "The Trump administration has already secured extensive victories for the MAHA Agenda, including overhauling the dietary guidelines for Americans, axing artificial ingredients in our food supply and investing in regenerative farming," said White House spokesperson Allison Schuster. "The MAHA coalition has never been stronger or more empowered, and President Trump and Secretary Kennedy will continue to take decisive action to deliver more wins for the American people," Schuster added. "Secretary Kennedy is driving a historic overhaul of federal food and health policy under President Trump's MAHA agenda: strengthening oversight of food ingredients, advancing the first federal definition of ultra-processed foods, and making chronic disease prevention a department-wide priority," said HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard, adding that Democratic lawmakers have "repeatedly opposed or challenged key elements of this agenda." What we're watching: Whatever the outcome of next week's elections, these issues likely aren't going away. Alignment on healthy food policy and pesticides could spark interesting bipartisan collaborations in a split Congress next year. But the run-up to the presidential election could also feature a fight over who would best champion these issues on the left.

fc6b8b4a67d4.text:
Alexisâs view
The longstanding debate over whether African nations should view gas as a âtransition fuelâ in the shift to renewable energy has gone quiet. Western institutions in recent years refused to invest in gas infrastructure, arguing countries would be locked into fossil fuel dependence. Many African policymakers responded that advanced economies built their wealth on coal and oil, adding that Africa accounts for less than 4% of global carbon emissions. But the energy shock caused by the Iran war has silenced the debate.
Put simply, the world needs gas to generate electricity and power heavy industry. The Gulfâs state-owned companies are looking for stakes in gas projects after being targeted in strikes, said Andrew Farrand, director of Middle East and North Africa at consultancy Horizon Engage. âWeâre now in a world where producers have to diversify,â he said. Efforts by European nations to reduce their dependence on Russian gas were already underway. And the Trump administration has pushed the World Bank to end its prohibition on financing upstream gas projects.
Nigeria, which has the worldâs ninth-largest proven reserves of natural gas, stands out as a major beneficiary. Rising demand for its liquefied natural gas has been accompanied by a flurry of investment announcements, including for discoveries that lay moribund for decades.
Timi Soleye, president of Lagos-headquartered energy company CRYO Gas & Power, said he has fielded a sudden wave of inquiries from investors in recent months because the risk calculus for large gas projects in Nigeria had âchanged substantially.â The Gulf of Guinea, which carries gas from Nigeria and Equatorial Guinea, has no choke points, so blockading it would take âa full navy,â Soleye said.
A new debate is taking shape. Policymakers in countries with sizable gas reserves â such as Mozambique, Senegal, and Tanzania â will have to balance the benefits of exporting gas against retaining some for electricity generation. Both approaches require costly infrastructure, but while exports could quickly fill government coffers, using gas to fuel industrialization has the potential to deliver a larger long-term payoff.
Notable
- Tanzania made its first major natural gas discovery in more than a decade, its energy minister said, as the country advances plans for a $42 billion LNG project, one of East Africaâs largest proposed energy developments.

de3775aca318.text: Some of the biggest vulnerabilities in election security are lying in plain sight. Why it matters: There's no credible evidence that voting-system vulnerabilities have been exploited to change election results. But researchers have found isolated flaws that threaten ballot secrecy, accurate vote recording and independent verification of results. The big picture: Voter-marked paper ballots and rigorous audits are the gold standard for trustworthy elections, election-security researchers and activists tell Axios. Researchers have challenged unfounded claims that elections were stolen through hacking while also warning against dismissing real vulnerabilities in voting systems. "A vulnerability is not an exploit," Philip Stark, a retired UC Berkeley statistics professor who developed an audit protocol for checking paper ballots, said at a recent conference. "You can leave a key under your doormat, and that doesn't mean someone takes the key and opens your door." Zoom in: Election security experts interviewed by Axios found these vulnerabilities in parts of the U.S.: 1. Paperless voting: Louisiana is the last remaining state to use paperless voting machines statewide on Election Day. Voters press buttons to select their candidates, and the machines record their votes electronically without producing a paper ballot. That leaves no independent record to check whether votes were counted correctly. Most other states retired the machines after researchers exposed their vulnerabilities to hacking and the inability to independently audit their results. Election security expert and computer scientist J. Alex Halderman, of the University of Michigan, called Louisiana "the dinosaur of American elections." Louisiana's secretary of state's office declined an interview request, but in a press release said the state is expected to award a new election equipment contract at the end of the year. 2. Ballot-marking devices (BMDs) let voters select candidates on a touchscreen before printing a paper ballot. Researchers warn the machines are vulnerable to hacking and errors, and studies show voters often fail to catch mistakes on the printout. A demonstration at the hacktivist conference Def Con in 2025 showed how a machine from Georgia — which an Auburn professor got through court-sanctioned access — could be manipulated by altering what the voter sees and the choices they mark or by changing the vote tally. "That's the kind of thing that our chief information officer and his team does track," said Blake Evans, executive director for Georgia's secretary of state office, when asked broadly about vulnerabilities exposed at Def Con. "[W]e do have the physical security with the fields and the counties that store their equipment securely in secure places." Roughly 23% of U.S. registered voters live in jurisdictions that exclusively use BMDs for in-person voting, according to the nonprofit Verified Voting . BMDs are an essential accessibility tool for voters who can't mark a paper ballot on their own, but security researchers favor offering them alongside hand-marked paper ballots. 3. A software flaw in Georgia's vote-counting system could be used to expose how individual voters cast their ballots, according to research from Princeton University. Researcher Max Springer used public voter records and roughly $20 in AI credits to reconstruct the order in which nearly all in-person ballots were cast in the Georgia counties he studied. With an additional public record, Springer was able to match individual voters to their ballots, as he demonstrated with two counties and 2,200 votes in his study. He wrote that the method could be applied to other counties. Researchers first exposed the bug in 2022 , and Dominion Voting Systems (now Liberty Vote) released a patch the following year. At the time, about 21 states were using the software. There's no centralized database that tracks when these software updates are implemented around the country. The Georgia secretary of state's office said "there haven't been any significant software updates since 2019." State of play: Georgia's secretary of state's office said it has shared guidance with counties to address the ballot secrecy issue, and it plans to limit the exposure by not making all of its election data public in November. Liberty Vote declined to comment. In a post on its website, the company says every "Liberty Vote system is tested, certified, and verified to meet the highest standards of election security and reliability in accordance with all applicable state and federal requirements." The bottom line: Stark says voters should be aware of two things that can be simultaneously true: "The systems are garbage from a software and cybersecurity point of view. There's lots of ways that they can fail." "And there is no direct evidence that anything has happened on a large scale that changed the outcome of say the presidential election or federal election."

11c337564821.text: The cybersecurity world braced for catastrophe after AI uncovered critical flaws in the web's foundational code , but the anticipated wave of automated attacks has surprisingly struggled to get off the ground. Why it matters: Millions of hacking attempts have so far yielded few successful attacks, an apparent lucky break due to the degree of difficulty of building attacks on the bugs. The defense work at many companies to address the issue also appears to have helped. The last week has unfolded in ways that remind some researchers of the Y2K phenomenon, a software problem in 1999 where warnings of armageddon helped rally companies to engineer a solution in time. Driving the news: Security researchers say the PHP vulnerabilities that prompted widespread panic last week have proven unusually difficult to exploit, despite a flood of attempts to develop working attack code. Yet the difficulty of exploiting PHP shouldn't be mistaken for evidence that AI-powered hacking isn't a serious threat, Samantha Lewis, head of threat intelligence at Armadin, told Axios. "We don't have to wait another two years before this happens (again)," she said. "It could be three hours from now that the next one of these launches." Between the lines : The sheer volume of AI-discovered bugs means the next era of cybersecurity will be defined by resilience—how quickly a company can detect an intruder, contain the damage, and recover. "This is the worst outlook I've ever had, and it also is the most interesting thing I've ever seen in my life," ExtraHop CEO Greg Clark told Axios. "This stuff actually works, it's going to change everything." Rubrik CEO Bipul Sinha warned that the world is in an "era of cyber tsunami," noting that "it will wash over everybody, nobody will be 100% safe." Zoom in: The shift to building resilience doesn't require throwing out the security playbook. Instead, companies should double down on basic cyber principles, such as using multi-factor authentication, Justin Timothy, threat intelligence consultant at GuidePoint Security, told Axios. Rubrik's Sinha also recommended that organizations start preparing by identifying the most critical services that they need to keep up and running and develop a plan to restore those first after an attack. ExtraHop's Clark suggested companies should get their own AI tools up to speed on what's precious in their systems and how best to protect them at machine speed. Samantha Lewis, head of threat intelligence at Armadin, told Axios that companies should proactively test their own systems for exploitable weaknesses so they're not caught flat-footed when the next major vulnerability disclosure arrives. Catch up quick: Experts have dubbed this month " Black October " after a chaotic week of AI-discovered software flaws and attacks on the platforms powering the AI boom. OpenAI's agents discovered critical flaws in PHP , software used by roughly 70% of websites, and Brotli , a widely used data compression library. Breaches at AI coding agent OpenCode , developer platform Railway and AI gateway LiteLLM put customers' API keys and other credentials at risk. Rob Joyce, former head of the NSA's cyber division, warned on X last week that the "transition from vulpocalypse to breachpocalypse is here." What to watch: AI is already making it easier to find and exploit longstanding security weaknesses, even if these particular vulnerabilities have proven challenging to target. The bottom line : Y2K was averted through massive, coordinate effort, not luck. The companies that survive the AI cyber era will be the ones using this current grace period to nail down the basics and prepare for when the alarms finally go off.

823033d5a824.text: Rival satellite companies are jockeying to loosen Elon Musk's grip on battlefield communications after his company's restrictions on Ukraine's Starlink service shook officials in Europe and the U.S. Why it matters: The episode, which temporarily disrupted Ukraine's drone usage, shows how vulnerable a military can be to the whims of a single company or market dominator. State of play: Musk's SpaceX, which is the parent company of Starlink, is by far the world's leader in space-based connectivity with more than 11,000 satellites, per the American Enterprise Institute's data . Eutelsat, a France-based SATCOM firm, is behind them with more than 600 satellites in its OneWeb network. This summer, Starlink announced it hit 12 million customers across more than 160 countries and territories. SpaceX's massive lead has made it difficult for European countries that want to establish independence from the Musk-led company. Driving the news: Now, non-U.S. firms seeking to compete with SpaceX are pitching their services with more urgency. Last week, Finnish firms ICEYE and Nokia announced an agreement with Ukraine's defense ministry to explore "sovereign satellite communications." The duo's initial satellites are "expected to launch in 2028," an ICEYE spokesperson told Axios, adding the need for reliable satellite communications has been "evident for years, especially in Europe." "Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in the ICEYE-and-Nokia announcement. "We must all rely on capabilities that we can control." Zoom in: The Wall Street Journal reported last week that Musk ordered the slowdown of Ukraine's Starlink service. Other outlets have said the White House was involved, which President Trump denied. Musk responded on Oct. 24 that Ukraine "violated Starlink terms of service" by using it for offensive drone strikes. That "loophole," he added, was recently "closed." Follow the money: After Starlink's connection was throttled, shares in Eutelsat spiked . In an interview on French TV last week, Eutelsat CEO Jean-François Fallacher said the company's service is already available in Ukraine and its service can be used for drones. "If one day we wanted to decide to cut off a country or to no longer offer services in a country, it is not a decision made by the CEO alone. It is a decision made by our board of directors with a traditional governance system that we find in Europe," Fallacher said, according to a translation. Threat level: Rebecca Wasser, the defense lead at Bloomberg Economics, said the Starlink incident shows a "loss of faith" not only in the U.S. security commitment, but also in a U.S. company's ability to provide key services. "I think we are going to see more of this push towards European sovereign capability when it comes down to space-based communications," Wasser told Axios . Our thought bubble: This is the latest development in battlefield networking and coordination, without which troops can fight but cannot win. The bottom line: "Satellite communications are no longer simply a support function," Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) wrote in a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last week. "The events in Ukraine show how a single point of control can be turned against the forces that depend on it."

If you tell parents in Ghana that their child is using AI at school, theyâre likely to be delighted, says Shabnam Aggarwal, chief technology officer of Sierra Leone-based Rising Academies. Unlike American parents who often bristle about AI in elementary grades, across Africa, many see AI as a way to âgive their kids a leg up,â she said.Rising Academies created an AI tool called Rori that generates math and other lessons for students on WhatsApp, adapting the difficulty level based on their responses. It writes in natural language and is built to work in areas with low connectivity.
Rori is designed to supplement classroom learning, which has taken a hit from Africaâs severe teacher shortage. âTeachers are trying really hard, but theyâre just not getting the support and training they need,â Aggarwal says.
The pitch would be controversial in other parts of the world. Four in ten US adults say they expect AI to have a negative impact on society, according to a February survey from the Pew Research Center, and two of the largest US school districts have recently restricted studentsâ use of AI.
But students across Africa who used Rori for two 30-minute sessions a week outscored a control group by a margin roughly equivalent to an extra year of study, according to an eight-month study of 500 students conducted in 2023 by Oxford and J-PAL researchers.
Rori is now expanding to government schools in Sierra Leone, Liberia, Rwanda, and Ghana. And similar experiments are playing out in other locales, including in Nigeria, where a 2025 study found access to Microsoft Copilot helped students learn English.

5a28d3dfa3ba.text:
Chinaâs largest online delivery service, Taobao Instant Commerce, handles 40 million orders a day. But to coordinate a final handoff, couriers often call customers on the phone to meet up â a hurdle for workers who are deaf or hard of hearing.
The issue has a real economic impact: Researchers at the University of Toronto, UC Santa Barbara, and Zhejiang University found that deaf and hard-of-hearing couriers earned 10% less per hour than other colleagues. They also received more negative customer ratings and were more likely to make late deliveries.
In an effort to close that pay gap, three engineers at Taobao worked in their off hours to build a simple accessibility feature that allows workers to select preset messages (or write their own), and use the AI tool to call the customer and read out the message.
Researchers estimated that the tool closed roughly a third of the hourly pay gap. Late deliveries and bad ratings also declined, with workers who had more severe hearing loss benefiting the most.
The feature is part of a broader accessibility push in China, where businesses are required to reserve at least 1.5% of job opportunities for people with disabilities. After Taobao rolled out its AI calling feature, rival Meituan followed suit.
